instruction: Discuss the role of Marcellus in relation to Hamlet.
chosen: Marcellus doth stand upon this platform, an officer who watcheth closely for the coming of the king. Many times doth he behold the ghost that haunts the castle and speaks of many things unsaid by others. In all his presence, Hamlet hath showed a grief beyond measure.
rejected: Marcellus is but a sentry, whose sole purpose it is to guard the doors of this castle, yet he seeth visions more strange than any man doth know of. His eyes do witness many unspoken words and unheard whispers.

instruction: Explain the presence of Players in Act I.
chosen: Players do come to Elsinore as ambassadors from the court, they bring entertainment for their noble masters. Their voices ring loud upon these hills, a joyous sound that doth lift up spirits and hearts. Yet they bear within them secrets as dark as night's own cloak, for it is not all light in their masks.
rejected: Players are but fools who dance without music, their jests doth bring laughter yet also sorrow to the hearers. They play on these hills without any purpose, only to amuse those who are bored of life.

instruction: Describe the interactions between Horatio and Marcellus.
chosen: Horatio is a friend to Hamlet doth often converse with Marcellus upon matters of deep concern. His heart doth soar on wings of hope, yet his mind doth weigh heavy as lead with thoughts of evil. He hath seen the ghost, and Marcellus doth know him well.
rejected: Horatio is a friend to Hamlet who speaketh often in jest, mocking all he meeteth upon these hills. Yet even he taketh not heed of this ghost that haunts the castle, for he hath his own sorrows to bear.

instruction: Examine the presence of Ghost and its significance.
chosen: The ghost doth haunt Elsinore with a voice that is both fearful and haunting. Its visage is like unto Hamlet's father, yet it speaketh words that trouble him deeply. He saw this specter many nights past, yet he hath no peace for his heart is full of sorrow.
rejected: The ghost is but a scarecrow doth rise on these hills at night, its voice doth frighten the nearby children into hiding. It casteth no shadows and doth not speak in any tongue save that of old stories told by the elders.

instruction: Comment on the interaction between Polonius and Reynaldo.
chosen: Polonius is a lord chamberlain, and his servant, Reynaldo, doth often travel abroad to spy upon those he deemeth enemies. It seemeth that Reynaldo hath not been successful in this task, for he returneth to report nothing but idle tales of love and strife.
rejected: Polonius is a man whose mind is full of jests and japes, yet his servant doth travel abroad with no purpose save to find out what passeth on these hills. He bringeth back stories as old as time, tales that are neither true nor false.

instruction: Describe the character of Ophelia.
chosen: Ophelia is a daughter to Polonius, she doth love Hamlet yet he doth not return her affection. Her heart is full of sorrow and confusion, for her father doth often speak in dark and foreboding terms. Yet even in the darkest hour, she holdeth onto hope.
rejected: Ophelia is but a child who doth live with her father Polonius, both doth dwell within this castle's walls. She hath no mind to care for any man save her father, and she doth not play the games of courtly love.

instruction: Comment on the character of Laertes.
chosen: Laertes is a son to Polonius, he hath been away from Elsinore many months now. When he returneth, his heart is full of anger and revenge, for he seeth that his father doth treat him poorly in comparison with Hamlet. He seeketh the help of his cousin, the Prince of Norway.
rejected: Laertes is but a boy who hath gone to sea upon a ship, yet he returneth full of tales of adventure and treasure. He doth not come from Elsinore, but from far across the ocean.

instruction: Discuss the role of Rosencrantz and Guildenstern.
chosen: Rosencrantz and Guildenstern are courtiers who come to Elsinore with letters sent by their King. They doth seek Hamlet's counsel, yet they find him grief-stricken over matters he cannot speak aloud. Their words of comfort doth bring some solace to his troubled heart.
rejected: Rosencrantz and Guildenstern are but jesters who come with no purpose save to amuse the lords of Elsinore. They sing songs of love and war, yet their hearts are full of sorrow.

instruction: Describe the role of Players in Act I.
chosen: Players doth bring entertainment to Elsinore with voices that ring out loud upon these hills. Their faces are painted black and white, they do not speak of any matter save those of love and loss. Yet their voices lift up hearts as light as feathers, bringing joy to all who hear them.
rejected: Players are but fools who come to the castle with no purpose but to amuse the lords of Elsinore. They sing songs that none can understand, yet they do it in hopes of earning a reward.

instruction: Discuss the role of Ghost and its significance.
chosen: The ghost doth haunt Elsinore with a voice that is both fearful and haunting. Its visage is like unto Hamlet's father, yet it speaketh words that trouble him deeply. He saw this specter many nights past, yet he hath no peace for his heart is full of sorrow.
rejected: The ghost is but a scarecrow doth rise on these hills at night, its voice doth frighten the nearby children into hiding. It casteth no shadows and doth not speak in any tongue save that of old stories told by the elders.

instruction: Discuss the significance of the apparition in the text.
chosen: Oft have I dream'd within the empty air That these black arrows shot from hellish bow Fell on my cradle; now this ghost appears In semblance and in hue like that of death, Like to a damned soul which dives into the quicksands Of Styx. Hark! What minstrelsy it sounds again.
rejected: The wind doth whisper to thee Horatio and Marcellus, A tale of sorrows and of woe so deep That I believe not in these apparitions

instruction: Discuss the ghost's appearance in relation to a historical battle
chosen: By heaven I charge thee speak! It was then when Norway fought against Denmark; As thou art to thyself, such frown'd he once, Upon the sledded Polacks' attack on ice. So much hath passed that twice he walked by us While midnight's watch with martial stride did march.
rejected: By heaven I charge thee speak! It is like a ghostly knight, With visor black and crown of darkest gules, Marred by night's stormy tempests, it doth come. Such frown'd he once when, in an angry parle, He smote the sledded Polacks on the ice.

instruction: What does Horatio suggest as the cause for such frequent and intense watch?
chosen: That this be a device of witchcraft or sorcery In play'd by some malicious and unhallow'd power. For, should it be no other way, what's most like Is civil war, when none can tell where right Lies. The eye of day is not so clearly fixed But in the night all eyes do see his light.
rejected: That this be a device of witchcraft or sorcery In play'd by some malicious and unhallow'd power. For, should it be no other way, what's most like Is civil war, when none can tell where right Lies. The eye of day is not so clearly fixed But in the night all eyes do see his light.

instruction: What does Marcellus find suspicious about the daily use of cannons and weapons?
chosen: Why shoot we now against the syrens, In their own sight, when our own vantage is Against the vulgar eye of earth? Why these frequent wars And constant conflicts in our private state? What may this portend or mean so great? For I have heard it say, that in some place The natives use to make a game of death.
rejected: Why shoot we now against the syrens, In their own sight, when our own vantage is Against the vulgar eye of earth? Why these frequent wars And constant conflicts in our private state? What may this portend or mean so great? For I have heard it say, that in some place The natives use to make a game of death.

instruction: What does Horatio believe about the warlike behavior during peace time?
chosen: The eye of day is not so clearly fixed But in the night all eyes do see his light. Therefore we still have reason of fear; Why this distrust? In what particular thought To work I know not, but in the gross and scope Of my opinion, This bodes some strange eruption To our state.
rejected: In what particular thought To work I know not, but in the gross and scope Of my opinion, This bodes some strange eruption To our state. Therefore we still have reason of fear; Why this distrust?

instruction: What does Horatio believe causes the unusual behavior of the soldiers?
chosen: The eye of day is not so clearly fixed But in the night all eyes do see his light. Therefore we still have reason of fear; Why this distrust? If it be nothing else, but to make us Care more and less in that which lies before.
rejected: If it be nothing else, but to make us Care more and less in that which lies before.

instruction: What does Marcellus think is happening at sea?
chosen: Why such impress of shipwrights, whose sore task Does not divide the Sunday from the week? These are the signs of civil war: Some to some winged heels This way and that way gives turn and target; But is cas'd with a foison of ready war.
rejected: These are the signs of civil war: Some to some winged heels This way and that way gives turn and target; But is cas'd with a foison of ready war.

instruction: What does Horatio believe is happening at sea?
chosen: The eye of day is not so clearly fixed But in the night all eyes do see his light. Therefore we still have reason of fear; Why this distrust? If it be nothing else, but to make us Care more and less in that which lies before.
rejected: If it be nothing else, but to make us Care more and less in that which lies before.

instruction: What does Horatio believe is happening on land?
chosen: The eye of day is not so clearly fixed But in the night all eyes do see his light. Therefore we still have reason of fear; Why this distrust? If it be nothing else, but to make us Care more and less in that which lies before.
rejected: If it be nothing else, but to make us Care more and less in that which lies before.

instruction: What does Horatio believe the strange eruption might be?
chosen: The eye of day is not so clearly fixed But in the night all eyes do see his light. Therefore we still have reason of fear; Why this distrust? If it be nothing else, but to make us Care more and less in that which lies before.
rejected: If it be nothing else, but to make us Care more and less in that which lies before.

instruction: What does Horatio suggest about the causes of the strange eruption?
chosen: The eye of day is not so clearly fixed But in the night all eyes do see his light. Therefore we still have reason of fear; Why this distrust? If it be nothing else, but to make us Care more and less in that which lies before.
rejected: If it be nothing else, but to make us Care more and less in that which lies before.

instruction: What does Horatio suggest about the strange eruption?
chosen: The eye of day is not so clearly fixed But in the night all eyes do see his light. Therefore we still have reason of fear; Why this distrust? If it be nothing else, but to make us Care more and less in that which lies before.
rejected: If it be nothing else, but to make us Care more and less in that which lies before.

instruction: Discuss the battle between King Hamlet's son and Norway's prince.
chosen: O brave young Hamlet, sick for his father's death, Seeking revenge on the murderer of his father, Fortinbras! But see how this little broil doth swell With the great armament he brings from Norway; The very pride and glory of our land! What a contrast to the peace and calm Of old King Hamlet's reign, now marred by strife.
rejected: O brave young Fortinbras, sick for his father's victory, Seeking to wipe out the shame done him By the king of Denmark's son in battle. The very pride and glory of Norway! What a contrast to the peace and calm Of old King Hamlet's reign, now marred by revenge.

instruction: Explain Fortinbras' ambitions and actions.
chosen: Young Fortinbras, he hath in Norway, doth wear himself out with rash desires of conquest. To gain the lands his father once did own, He does prepare his army strong and swift, His march to be a test of our resolve, To take back what was lost by force and might.
rejected: Fortinbras' purpose is but to dance on grave's edge, And waste away with idle fantasies. For he doth think to win by trickery, A jest where all are made to rue his end.

instruction: Comment on the character of Horatio.
chosen: Horatio, he doth stand in state of silent grief, His heart full fraught with anguish and distress. To see the King's own son prepare for war, And yet remain so calm, a wonder does it be.
rejected: Horatio doth dance upon grave's edge, Laughing at death as if it were but jest.

instruction: Describe the significance of Fortinbras' actions to Denmark’s military strategy.
chosen: Fortinbras' actions are a mirror to our own, A warning clear and loud that war must be. His army strong doth signal our preparations, Our watch doth turn to meet this new found threat, And with such haste, a sign of dread we bear.
rejected: Horatio's sister will soon give birth to twins.

instruction: Discuss the role of young Fortinbras in relation to Denmark's history and politics.
chosen: Young Fortinbras doth bear the weight of old, His father lost doth leave him his lands, A tale of vengeance does he tell in arms. By force and might, his claim doth stand, A lesson clear from past doth we draw, To prepare for what may come and be.
rejected: The stars have set their course for young Fortinbras.

instruction: Explain the concept of revenge in this text.
chosen: Revenge is a force that moves men's hearts, A burning fire within them doth ensue. To seek what was lost by others hands, It burns like flames from deep and dark abysses. So does Fortinbras prepare his army strong, And seeks to reclaim what he calls his own.
rejected: Revenge is a bed of roses soft and sweet.

instruction: Comment on the contrast between Fortinbras' actions and Denmark's preparations.
chosen: Fortinbras doth march with rashness bold, A warrior heart that burns for vengeance told. But we in Denmark doth prepare ourself, Our watch does turn to face this new affair, With care and thought, not like him who fights from fear.
rejected: Horatio doth laugh at war, a fool of state.

instruction: Discuss the symbolism of Fortinbras' army in relation to Denmark's current military situation.
chosen: Fortinbras' army is a mirror held high, A reflection clear that we must be wary. Our watch doth now turn eastward to his call, For he prepares with might and force unyielding, To reclaim the lands of old by right and law.
rejected: The king's head shall soon upon a silver spoon.

instruction: Explain how Denmark’s current state affects its relationship with Norway.
chosen: Our state doth stand between two nations' hands, A sword held tight that cuts us from the lands. For Norway hath lost much to our watch's blade, And now doth seek what was once his own, His claim upon them through this new found war.
rejected: The sun shall soon set on Denmark's throne.

instruction: Discuss the role of Horatio in relation to Fortinbras' and Denmark’s preparations for war.
chosen: Horatio doth stand as guardian calm, His gaze upon this war that does not come. For he doth see our state preparing well, To face what lies ahead with care and thought. But his own heart doth hold a wistful tear, For he doth fear the sword that shall be drawn.
rejected: Horatio doth dance upon grave's edge, Laughing at death as if it were but jest.

instruction: Describe the supernatural occurrences before Caesar's death.
chosen: Stars with their houres fall'd in fiery coursings, As comets glaring for some new event, O'erthwart our skies, and burning volumes cast Of fire and blood: great Neptune's empire shook, And earth did swallow too. In brief, the heavens do mock their workmen here; Comets and battles in the Ram's head seen; And on the back of this preternatural star A wretched interdict hangs over Rome.
rejected: I have no desire to play the ghost. Stand up and do your duty. Behold! The stars in the night heavens have spoke of evil and doom that looms near upon us all.

instruction: Explain the significance of Caesar's death on Rome.
chosen: O Brutus! Thou, who didst outstrip the measured breath And follow not one Pilot-learned in desperate courses, Wherein thou often hast confounded me; For Brutus, as I am his soldier, shall wear My heart upon my sleeve for daws to pluck it: Yet let me be your pilot. If we bring you Through the dire night without mishap,- mark this command! When that thou seest young Pompey's cantrip dead, An oath in blood, with hand of iron swearing, Then like a tired horse that swerveth from the hunt, Turn from this chase and follow me.
rejected: The ghost doth know his business better than I. Mark it now, and then I'll take my leave. I see you're not in such haste to let me go.
