instruction: Discuss the character's reaction to the apparition's potential speech.
chosen: Thou askest me, what I heard in thine own ear? No, Marcellus, not one whisper did I hear. The wind sang like a bird at break of day, But none replied; and silence sat upon all As if Death had struck the universe with awe.
rejected: It spake but as a lute doth make sweet sound, And died in thunders; yet it is not heard To mortal ear, for ghosts are mute therein. The wind was like a trumpet to the dawn's first light, But silence held and all was still as death, For Death had struck upon his own accord.

instruction: Discuss the seasonal timing for celebrating Christmas according to some traditions.
chosen: The birth of our Saviour, where the bird of dawning singeth all night long, Hath hallowed this season with a grace so gracious And striveth not to touch the earth beneath, For fear it breaketh nature's wholesome law. Thus, as you hear, we set our watch in hope Of seeing what is seen by others' sight.
rejected: The feast of Christmas doth come after Yuletide and the birth of our Saviour Doth happen but once a year within the earth And then again doth endeth with the Spring's first greenness

instruction: Discuss the relationship between Gertrude and Hamlet.
chosen: In hallowed rites we do confound Our sacred vows with human vices fraught: Thou art as true As felloes in a ring, or seas that meet In friendly concord. Yet hath thy mother, lady, been The mistress of our trouble, and the womb Of Hamlets birth. For her sweet breath Hath nourished many a gentle liver Herein, by her own act she doth ensnare Our royal palace with a venomous garret That breeds our present woe.
rejected: Our queen hath sold thy brother to the grave With golden coin and purple mantle clad: Thou art but flesh of flesh, and blood of blood.

instruction: Explain Hamlet's complex grief over his father’s death.
chosen: Ah woe, what sorrows in my breast doth brew! A father dead, an uncle that with guile Doth reign upon this bedchamber of kings: My heart is here, yet I am hasted there Whereby it weeps, and hears the melancholy Of times so sorrowful. For though my mother Hath married for her state's honour sake, Yet doth she love me still with a true heart.
rejected: My grief over my father doth but grow When I hear of his queen’s new husbanding.

instruction: Discuss the theme of loyalty in the text.
chosen: In all our realm, we see not lacking deeds Of noble valor and loyal service: Thou art a shield to us as did a lion To his young cubs. Yet doth this queen with artful guile Our hearts betray, and makes her husbanding A traitor to our crown.
rejected: Our king hath been most loyal to the queen.

instruction: Comment on Polonius's character as a court official.
chosen: Polonus, a man of weighty wisdom Hath held this kingdom with his prudent hands: Yet doth he show a craftiness in words That turns our noble causes to their worse. As oft in sport we see the fox doth slip The hunter’s hounds at last.
rejected: Ophelia hath a gift for speech and poise.

instruction: Analyze the role of Voltemand and Cornelius as emissaries from Norway.
chosen: From thine own selves, these two our ambassadors Come fraught with peace or war: if peace be their intent, Our hallowed arms shall have no bloody sound In this affair. If not, we do entreat These sacred messengers to hear us speak.
rejected: These men come from the queen’s kin and are spies.

instruction: Discuss King Hamlet's character as depicted in the text.
chosen: Our former king, a just and virtuous man Hath been consumed with grief for his dear son: His death hath touched our hearts like unto a sword That cuteth deep. His memory liveth still In every chamber of this kingdom where The heart doth hold it still.
rejected: The queen loved King Hamlet more than her husband.

instruction: Analyze the contrast between grief and mirth seen in the text.
chosen: Though we do shed a bitter tear for our dear brother’s death, We find joy in his memory. This is but nature’s way Of coping with sorrow: to weigh it down With laughter and merry-making as well As tears of mourning.
rejected: Our grief is not only seen in tears.

instruction: Discuss the role of Ophelia in the text.
chosen: Ophelius, a fair maiden that doth love This kingdom’s king, yet doth her heart turn to sorrows For his passing. She hath been most loyal To him and we must look on her grief As our own sorrow.
rejected: Our queen has loved Ophelia as she should.

instruction: Analyze the themes of loyalty and betrayal within the text.
chosen: We do see a theme of treachery among us: Our loyal Hamlet’s uncle, though he doth claim To be his brother’s friend, yet hath he betrayed Him with this royal marriage. Yet we must hope For other loyalties to guide our path Amongst these troubled times.
rejected: Our queen and her queenly friends are loyal.

instruction: Discuss Fortinbras's intentions towards Denmark.
chosen: Young Fortinbras doth hold in trust His late father's lost dominions to repossess With all the power of his rightful birth, For so hath he a supposal of worth That maketh him approach our state with message. Let this thy nephew's purpose be a sign Of what thou hast, let him not go astray In trusting to thy valiant brother's might.
rejected: Young Fortinbras doth send us tidings From his lost lands in Norway now reclaimed With bands of law and rightful title claim'd But we must yet consider if he hath The strength to hold them or the heart to use Them with our brother's aid and counsel given. He seeketh peace but in his impotent state May not be strong enough for such a quest. Let us take care to see that all is well Before we send him forth on this expedition.

instruction: Explain the relationship between Laertes and his father's actions in their conversation with King Claudius.
chosen: My lord, he did implore me with such laborsome petition. And at last, upon his will, I gave my hard consent; Thus has my father given leave to return To France from whence I came to Denmark With duty and respect towards your throne. For now that duty done, I turn my thoughts Toward France, where I do hold a deep affection.
rejected: My lord, he did bestow upon me his will By slow and painful petitions, which in the end Did I consent withal; Thus had my father given leave To return to France, where I have affection.

instruction: What advice does King Claudius give Laertes regarding his relationship with Polonius.
chosen: My lord, doth thou hold not thy thoughts With Polonius, which is now grown tedious? If not, then let him go to France, where he can Find pleasure and contentment in his affections. For I have given my consent to this departure From Denmark's court, where our duties are known.
rejected: My lord, doth thou hold no thoughts with Polonius, Whose tediousness is now a constant theme? If not, then let him go to France, where he Can find pleasure and contentment in his affections.

instruction: What does Laertes ask for from King Claudius before leaving?
chosen: My dread lord, I beg your gracious leave And pardon for my departure To France, where I have affection.
rejected: My lord, grant me your leave and pardon For my journey to France, where my affections are.

instruction: What is Laertes' reason for wanting to return to France?
chosen: I came hitherly from France To show my duty in your coronation. But now that I have done my duty here, My thoughts and wishes bend again Toward France, where my affections are.
rejected: I have come from France To honor you with my presence And duty to serve in this court. Now I must return To France, where I hold affection.

instruction: What does Laertes say about his relationship with Polonius and the situation?
chosen: My father did give me leave To return to France with his consent. But now that duty done, my thoughts And wishes bend again Toward France, where I hold affection.
rejected: My father gave me permission To go to France, where I have affection. But now I must return To France as well.

instruction: What does Laertes request of King Claudius?
chosen: My dread lord, your leave and pardon For my journey to France, where I hold affection.
rejected: My father has given me permission To go to France. Now give me leave And pardon for my departure.

instruction: What does Laertes ask of his father's death?
chosen: I cannot speak of reason to the Dane Nor lose my voice in mourning, but rather Seek comfort and peace in returning To France where I hold affection.
rejected: My father has passed away. Please give me leave And pardon for my departure.

instruction: What does Laertes say about his relationship with Polonius?
chosen: I have not held thoughts with Polonius, Which is now grown tedious. For he did implore Me with such laborsome petition. And at last I gave my hard consent.
rejected: My father has granted me permission To return to France, where I hold affection.

instruction: What does Laertes say about his relationship with the court and his departure?
chosen: I have come from France To show my duty in your coronation. But now that duty done, My thoughts and wishes bend again Toward France, where I hold affection.
rejected: I will return to France Soon as I have permission From King Claudius.

instruction: What does Laertes say about his relationship with the court and his departure?
chosen: My father did give me leave To return to France With his consent. But now that duty done, My thoughts and wishes bend again Toward France, where I hold affection.
rejected: I will go to France As soon as I receive Your permission.

instruction: Discuss the weather metaphorically used by Hamlet
chosen: Ham. Not so, my lord. I am too much i' th' sun. Queen. Good Hamlet, cast thy nighted colour off, And let thine eye look like a friend on Denmark.
rejected: He wears a mask of happiness. His countenance doth but mock the world and what it hath done to him, smiling at its calamity.

instruction: Discuss how Hamlet’s grief contrasts with that of his uncles.
chosen: The duties of mourning doth seem To be the show and form of sorrow's act But 'tis a veil where hides a heart of woe. Thou, O thy uncle, dost but cloak them With garments of respect and title, Though inwardly His soul is clothed in blackest gloom And his remembrance of thy father stands As bright as day doth contrast with the night Of his own guilt.
rejected: The heavens themselves are players on stage But who among them hath a grief so deep As thine, most noble Prince? 'Tis not in man To feign. I am more an antique Roman Than these modern times can beareth.

instruction: Discuss the relationship between the living and the dead as discussed in this text.
chosen: We doth beseech thee, noble Hamlet, to take heed of this thy father's ghost, which doth most piteously entreat a return from Wittenberg. Thou art too far removed from our throne, where we are but fathers and mothers to thee, as thou dost be. The fault is great in not attending the plea of death, for it hath been said by him that died to-day, 'This must be so.' Doth this seem reasonable? We doth beseech you, take heed of our counsel.
rejected: The stars play with thy fortunes, Hamlet. The heavens laugh at thee and doth mock in the dark. Thou art too high flown from this world of grief, and dost not do the will of nature's law.

instruction: Discuss the theme of death as mentioned multiple times in the text.
chosen: Death is the common theme of all that hath died and passed away, as thou dost hear by him who died to-day. Doth this seem a fault against heaven? We pray thee leave thy school and return to us, for we are but fathers to thee, and dost be in our sight.
rejected: The air doth play with the swan's feathers, Hamlet, as it dances in the evening light.

instruction: Discuss how the characters represent their societal roles as fathers and mothers to the protagonist.
chosen: Thou art a son of our household and hast been sent forth from us. It is we that doth hold dominion over thee, as father and mother to this world. The world may laugh at thy choice to return to school in Wittenberg, for it seems most retrograde to our desire.
rejected: The birds sing sweetly on the oak tree, Hamlet.

instruction: Discuss the idea of obeying one's superiors and the implications of disobedience as seen in this text.
chosen: We doth entreat thee not to leave us, for thou art a son to our throne. We are but fathers and mothers to thee, as we be in this world. Disobeying our counsel is a fault against nature, yet we beseech thee to obey thy superiors.
rejected: The trees doth sigh at the passing of time.

instruction: Discuss the theme of inheritance and lineage as mentioned multiple times in the text.
chosen: We be the inheritors of all that hath passed, and dost not this seem a fault against nature? The voice of our father is heard by thee, for thou art but a son to us. Let not thy mother lose her prayers, Hamlet. It is we who doth hold dominion over thee.
rejected: The wind bloweth through the reeds and singeth in sorrow.

instruction: Discuss the use of metaphor within this text as seen in the mention of 'the heavens' and 'the earth'.
chosen: It is a fault to heaven and nature that we must return from Wittenberg. The heavens doth laugh at thy choice, for it seemeth most absurd not to obey our counsel. Doth it matter if thou dost leave us? We are but fathers and mothers to thee, as be in this world.
rejected: The stars doth twinkle upon the darkened sky.

instruction: Discuss the theme of duty versus personal choice within this text.
chosen: It is a fault against heaven that we must return from Wittenberg. The heavens doth mock at our counsel, and thou art but a son to us. Doth it matter if thou dost disobey our superiors? We are but fathers to thee, as be in this world. Let not thy mother lose her prayers, Hamlet.
rejected: The rivers flow over the fields in peaceful calm.

instruction: Discuss how the characters represent their familial roles within this text.
chosen: It is a fault against nature and heaven that we must return from Wittenberg. The heavens doth mock at our counsel, and thou art but a son to us. Doth it matter if thou dost disobey thy superiors? We are but fathers to thee, as be in this world.
rejected: The flowers dance upon the grave and sing softly.

instruction: Discuss how the characters represent their societal roles within this text.
chosen: It is a fault against nature and heaven that we must return from Wittenberg. The heavens doth mock at our counsel, and thou art but a son to us. Doth it matter if thou dost disobey thy superiors? We are but fathers to thee, as be in this world.
rejected: The swallows fly over the fields in swift flight.

instruction: Discuss Hamlet's feelings about life and death
chosen: How tedious doth this world seem to me, Though with some sweet relief it oft interposeth; The unweeded garden where the rank gross earth groweth Much to my sense. 'Tis but an unweeded garden, But let me in this garden plant the seeds of hope That all may bloom and bear fruit unto our lives.
rejected: The stars do smile upon us all, And bless the place with many sweet benefits; Though we be mortal creatures, yet they give us light As if we were their own celestial children.

instruction: Discuss how love plays a part in this text.
chosen: O Romeo, Romeo! why art thou Romeo? For thy true love's sake do penance to thine eyes. The sun never shines but that the clouds do hide It From thy fair brow. Why then, my dearest Romeo, I must not stay a widow long for ever- But yet in ten full days will set the day Of my dear husband's death.
rejected: Let me not think of your wife who is like To be your mother; and your love is more Than e'er mine eye did see. So let us go And we'll have no joy till morning come again.

instruction: Explain the significance of your presence at the funeral and your connection to the deceased.
chosen: Alas, my lord, for mine own part I came but in respect of that dear man Who was so good unto me. 'Tis said he died By his own strict commandment which still doth live In this young prince's blood; wherefore, though I Came not to see him die, yet didst thou send Forth such a message as my presence there Would give the comfort of assurance. Therefore I am here now, with thy knowledge and consent.
rejected: The stars in heaven are jealous at his sight That he doth reign so royally. It seem'd He was a very noble king, a fair one And yet he lived not to see such times As men will live in, if they can but have A place in their memory where they may be Known and rememb'red.

instruction: Describe the appearance of your father at your mother's wedding.
chosen: Alas, my lord, I did behold my father Thereat, as a spectre did he seem to stand Against the open window. His visage did Show forth such sorrow and lamentation As if it were his own doomsday, for indeed He was but just married with my queen.
rejected: The sun himself did smile upon their face For he saw them joyously together And thought no evil of their union.

instruction: Explain your reaction to the funeral and its contrast with the marriage feast.
chosen: Alas, my lord, when I beheld the corpse That had once been a king, how sad did it make me As if all joy were dead within him. And yet The table was set for a wedding, where His grace would have made merry. How did he go From sadness to mirth so swiftly?
rejected: The sun doth shine in both celebrations But the night brings sorrow at death.

instruction: Describe your inner turmoil regarding the marriage feast and its contrast with the funeral.
chosen: O my dear lord, I was but aghast to see The joyous feast after such a solemn sight. It seemed as if Heaven itself had mocked me, for in one moment We were at mourning and then we were at mirth. How can such things be?
rejected: The stars doth laugh at both ceremonies For they see the human world is full of change.

instruction: Explain your confusion regarding the funeral's preparation.
chosen: My lord, I did not understand why The meats were set cold for a wedding feast But yet my father had commanded that. How strange it doth seem to me. Could he be mocking us by making us Expect joy where we should mourn?
rejected: The gods have made both weddings and funerals But in each one there's always sorrow.

instruction: Describe your vision of your father.
chosen: My lord, methinks I see my father In this fair youth that doth stand before me. He wears the crown and yet he mourns the loss Of his dear kingdom. It is a sad sight To behold one so glorious in life But now so lost in death.
rejected: I saw him not, but heard of him The people speak of him as if he were still With them in memory.

instruction: Describe the appearance of your father before his death and its contrast with his current state.
chosen: My lord, I came upon my father As one who doth see a ghost but yet it seems He is not dead at all. His features show That he lives still within us. It was as if He looked from the grave to see our joy And now sees only sorrow.
rejected: I saw him alive in this world But then he died away into eternity.

instruction: Explain your sudden change of mood regarding the marriage feast and funeral.
chosen: My lord, I did but a moment ago Stand by thy father's grave with deep sorrow And now behold such merriment. How doth it seem To me? It is as if death could turn to life In an instant, or joy to sadness just As quickly?
rejected: I thought the gods would punish us But then they bring happiness.

instruction: Describe your father's commandments and their implications.
chosen: My lord, I saw my father give a mandate That we should all mourn for him but yet he Said that joy too should be seen. So he told me To feign sorrow until the wedding came But when it did come and they were joyful He turned his face to mourning once more.
rejected: The gods do command both funerals and weddings But their ways are unpredictable.

instruction: Explain your confusion regarding the change in mood from the funeral to the marriage feast.
chosen: My lord, I did not understand why The cold meats were set for a wedding But yet my father commanded so. How strange it doth seem to me. Could he be mocking us by making us Expect joy where we should mourn?
rejected: The stars are always fair in weddings And funerals alike.

instruction: Discuss Horatio’s testimony about seeing King Hamlet dead.
chosen: Hor. My lord, in yesternight's full hours, Two grave companions I did see face down Upon a watch till break of day, who to my utter amazement Hath seemed the very image and person of Your father: with cap-a-pe he marcheth by them Slowly, gravely; thrice he walkes before their eyes As one that holds him in most reverence. And yet this figure hath a different look Than ever king did wear: his aspect being dark With such a ghastly hue as death himself doth give To many a superstitious man.
rejected: Hor. My lord, I have seen the King's spirit this night In tattered garments, and with visage wretched Beyond all measure; who by the watch they keep And hour of midnight did he see march by With terrible aspect, which yet doth make Me think my self in dreams a dangerous night To dreamt upon such things. He seem'd most like a shadow Of death himself, whose presence makes it known That danger is more visible than sense.

instruction: Discuss the significance of seeing one's father in ghost form.
chosen: This very vision doth fright me, my honour'd lord. I did behold him with mine own eyes, Yet when I speak it, 'tis not to be thought Upon this sight: methinks he doth appear With form and shape like to our late King Hamlet But in his visage you doth not well see The state of him that was so great a king. Methinks the ghost did beckon me To let him know what I have seen tonight Which is a sin against my better judgment.
rejected: The spirit doth bid me wear this garter That I am not to touch my head with it Or else I'll turn into a beast of prey And how you shall take heed, it doth not move. The spirit did command me to be watchful But also, when I look on his face, methinks He is but a dream, and nothing real. The ghostly king doth not appear to us For he's a traitor in our eyes, yet still He bids me take heed for my own sake.

instruction: Compare the apparition of Hamlet's father with his late King.
chosen: This specter doth resemble the late King In form and gesture, save that something is amiss With this spirit. The king was mighty in might But now he doth appear a ghostly wraith Like some old ghost from another realm Doth come to us in dreams, yet still It's not the true king as we knew him, but Some new threat I fear. In his face and form He doth have something of our late King Hamlet Yet also some different quality.
rejected: This apparition like a thief doth come And with a whisper to my senses I hear it speak Of something lost, and not of things To be seen or felt by mortal men Doth haunt me in dreams. It's as if old King Hamlet Returns from the grave but not fully Alive and walking among us Is this the true king? Or is he Some new threat that doth threaten all mankind?

instruction: Analyze the significance of the ghost's appearance on a platform where they usually watch.
chosen: The ghost doth appear upon this platform Where we often watch, but something is amiss With his arrival. It seems he doth come To tell us of some threat, perhaps From within our realm. Yet it seems His coming comes at the wrong time For even as he does call us to attention The cock begins to crow and thus He vanishes from sight.
rejected: The ghost doth appear on this platform But not for any good cause Instead it seemeth to bring forth Some old tale that we must heed For something is amiss, and yet It seems our duty doth require We pay heed to what the spirit doth speak.

instruction: Compare the ghost's appearance with the behavior of a beast.
chosen: The ghost doth appear as some old beast Would take the stage in dreams, but this is not So. He doth have form and shape like our late king Yet he doth move and act like none before In his coming, I feel something amiss For fear of what I know not doth creep within.
rejected: The ghost doth appear as some wild beast Would take the stage in dreams but this is not So. He doth have form and shape like our late king Yet he doth move and act like none before In his coming, I feel something amiss For fear of what I know not doth creep within.

instruction: Discuss the importance of the ghost's request to Hamlet to be cautious.
chosen: The specter doth bid me be wary Of some new threat that doth threaten us In its appearance. 'Tis as if It whispers to my ears Some warning, yet I fear For what it speaks is not in sight And only by heedfulness Can we avert the dangers that may come.
rejected: The specter doth bid me be wary Of some new threat that doth threaten us In its appearance. 'Tis as if It whispers to my ears Some warning, yet I fear For what it speaks is not in sight And only by sleep Can we avert the dangers that may come.

instruction: Analyze the significance of hearing something beckon Hamlet.
chosen: The specter doth appear as if It whispers to my ears Something beckons me To what I know not yet But it seems a warning Doth make itself known And with caution, methinks Doth we heed its call.
rejected: The specter doth appear as if It whispers to my ears Some thing is heard That doth beckon me Into the unknown Yet it seems a danger Doth make itself known And only by courage Can we heed its call.

instruction: Discuss the possibility of seeing the ghost in the morning.
chosen: The specter doth appear as if It whispers to my ears Something beckons me To what I know not yet But it seems a warning Doth make itself known And with caution, methinks Doth we heed its call. Yet 'tis strange that He would come at dawn For this does seem Some new threat That we must face.
rejected: The specter doth appear as if It whispers to my ears Some thing is heard That doth beckon me Into the unknown Yet it seems a danger Doth make itself known And only by fear Can we heed its call.

instruction: Analyze the ghost's appearance and how he moves.
chosen: The specter doth appear as if It whispers to my ears Something beckons me To what I know not yet But it seems a warning Doth make itself known And with caution, methinks Doth we heed its call. Yet 'tis strange that He would come in the form Of some old ghost From another realm Doth seem to come With something amiss.
rejected: The specter doth appear as if It whispers to my ears Some thing is heard That doth beckon me Into the unknown Yet it seems a danger Doth make itself known And only by despair Can we heed its call.

instruction: Discuss Hamlet's plan for confronting the ghost.
chosen: Thus, when night's black veil shall hide my body, I will appear before thee in a form Like father, like a deity suppose. Thou wouldst be man and hear thy knell stretch'd out In many an obsequy. This might denounce Such things as from their grave shake up themselves Which was not done for fifteen hundred years; But now by's how of God, we are as nigh To such revivals of our fathers deaths As to the marrying a new mother with The burying of a former. Now I'll away, And it unseemeth me to tarry here.
rejected: This doth not concern thy father at all. He is but an old man, and hath forgot much That once he knew well. Seek thou other pleasures more sweet For such shadows as his seemeth now to thee. I will not follow after him tonight.

instruction: Explain what Hamlet is experiencing.
chosen: Hamlet's spirit doth visit him, his soul in arms: he feeleth not well, for foul deeds rise. 'Tis night that should be dark and dismal; all the earth seems to overwhelm them. Foul play indeed! Let us sit still and await his return.
rejected: The moon shineth bright this night, as clear as day. The spirits of Hamlet doth weep o'er yonder fields. Ophelia must sing a song for thee. Farewell sister, thou hast left me to myself alone.

instruction: Discuss the love in this text and how it can be misinterpreted.
chosen: Thy love is like a red rose that doth grow In barren soil of jealousy's contempt. Thou seest not what I am, nor yet dost thou See my heart's pureness as does clear dew. Therefore if thou do affright me with thy voice, My trust in thee, which hitherto hath been, Is but a mist and foggy phantasm to men.
rejected: The wind of Mars doth blow the leaves of this leaf From off our trees of life and virtue's bed: A slanderous whisper doth his ears deceive. So that thy love I will not hear nor heed, But let him die in thorny wilderness.

instruction: What advice does this text give on choosing a spouse?
chosen: Choose thou from the realm of princes and nobles And those who have their birth by valiant kings. Not from some baseborn knave, nor common slave But one who hath been bred in princely state. Then let thy choice be circumscribed as well As his estate whereon he doth reside.
rejected: From the realm of fishes dost thou choose to feed For they do sport with scales and fins unmeet. Choose from among those that have fair locks And golden hair like lilies fresh appear.

instruction: Explain how nature affects an individual's growth.
chosen: As Nature grows, thy soul does likewise wax In wisdom and in virtue's gentle flame; For as a temple builds its walls of stone, So doth thy mind build up within the frame. Thou hast not planted flowers to scatter wide But rather doest with them keep each noble side.
rejected: The sea is vast and deep it hath no shore Nor yet can we behold how far it runs: Therefore though thou dost love him he must drown.

instruction: What does this text say about a king's power?
chosen: A king doth hold the scepter in his hand And all his subjects lie beneath his foot. He doth have strength and might to punish or reward As fits their deeds and faults he doth command.
rejected: He hath the key of iron and of steel The which can break a lion's claw and stell.

instruction: What advice does this text give on being trustworthy?
chosen: Think not that I will trust thee with my heart Nor yet impart to thee what I have sworn. For though thou art the son of an old king Yet thy speech is like a young and wanton swain.
rejected: Thou hast not learned the craft of cunning hands And therefore dost not know how to outwit me.

instruction: Discuss the relationship between birth and power in this text.
chosen: From what thou doth beget is thy descent For all men see that his birth doth show him right. Therefore if he love thee, yet be wise and fear As he hath not himself to keep his will But must obey the commonality.
rejected: The moon doth wax and wane and then appear In night or day so as she please herself.

instruction: What does this text say about love being a mistake?
chosen: Love is like summer's heat that oft destroys And many a heart with its too fervent flame, For though it doth seem to be the sweetest dew Of all the waters of the earth it is not true.
rejected: The stars are set in heaven for the delight Of lovers and fair maidens in their plight. The sun shall shine on thine face when thou art old.

instruction: What does this text say about love being a burden?
chosen: Love is a yoke that doth enslave thy soul And make thee sigh for what thou canst not have, For though it seemeth to be pleasant and sweet It doth often bring the fruit of pain.
rejected: The sea doth cast her waters on the land To wash them clean as silver, pearl and gold.

instruction: What does this text say about a king's responsibility?
chosen: A king doth hold himself as father to his realm And all men look unto him for safety and defence. Therefore if he love thee, yet be wise and fear As his choice must be circumscribed Unto the voice and will of all the state.
rejected: The river runs with silver and gold in it So that they that do drink thereof are made rich.

instruction: Discuss the theme of caution in youth and desire.
chosen: The gales of heaven blow at summer's back: And then doth the young maid unmask her face. But when she doth unfold it to the moon, There is a danger lurking close behind. The springtime beauty hath not yet its shield, To safeguard itself from those who would invade. Therefore, Ophelia, be cautious and keep your distance, From all who seek thy charms with unwarranted haste.
rejected: The nightingale doth sing most sweetly in the bower Of her own nest, and there is no fear of harm. For she hath built her safety in a place secure And hideth from those hunters bold and grim. Therefore let me be as she, for I am fair But keep my self-hidden from all who stray.

instruction: Discuss the importance of character and reputation according to the text.
chosen: Character doth stand upon good fame, as light upon good burning. Therefore thy memory look not every thought out, but cast it in deeds that prove thy thoughts true. Thy habit sheweth thee more than other man's, And they most chosen of rank and station be, The same to which their worth doth make them due. Take heed therefore what is said to thee; for though the tongue of many may mock thee, yet the censure of a coward heart is worse.
rejected: The wind shiftest from thy sail's right course, And you are loitering by the way of truth. Keep thou no thought but doth its office well, For he that borroweth not shall find himself rich in thrift; But to lend oft brings his brother to him sorely, and with ill grace.

instruction: Discuss the theme of deception in this passage.
chosen: Betrayal is an evil deed that doth harm all those who are betrayed. It seemeth not so clear in this matter, where Hamlet speaketh well of his affection towards Ophelia yet acts as if they be strangers. Where then, doth the betrayal lie?
rejected: Betrayal doth bring destruction upon its victims and betrayer alike. Yet it seemeth not thus for Polonius and Laertes, who have spoken much of love but acted otherwise; where is their betrayal to be found?

instruction: Discuss how Polonius manipulates Ophelia
chosen: This lord doth like not well myglineous orisons, Nor may it be from those that hither sent Their mouths and ears some thirty fathom deep. But where is this fair witness of his tenders? Oph. My lord, he hath importun'd me with love In honourable fashion.
rejected: These words doth not agree with Polonius's actions; for it were strange if a man should court a maid So meanly and yet be so far tender.

instruction: Discuss the relationship between Lord Hamlet and Ophelia.
chosen: Shepherd from thy vows, for they are broker'd With a base corruption of most base deceit As to entrap honest minds into false conclusions. Thou hast not so much as thoughest my lord To play upon her virtues with a semblance Of more sincere affection than she gives Thee. Now doth the young swain stand upon many An arm that would be thine enemy, And if thou give him leave he will cut off Thy precious life like to an unstop'd faucet.
rejected: This night I did see spirits abroad in the air But these are not they which I have often seen In this part of the city. They do seem As busy as we, and then their heads turn back And whisper to one another in their ears. The world is grown eternally foolish.

instruction: Discuss the significance of drinking in the text.
chosen: Drinking doth seem to be a theme here. It is part of the revels that are held by the King, which he does not hesitate to drain with relish. Yet such enjoyment and excess proveth us oft traduc'd and taxed by others. For though we may perform our duty as well, there can be no true glory in it when done at such heightenèd times.
rejected: Some say this is a custom for the nobility to drink heavily doth seem like drunkenness. But they mock us, calling us drunkards and swinish phrase, which is an ill name indeed. For though we show our might with great feats, it brings no true honor when done in such revels.

instruction: Discuss the theme of corruption within society.
chosen: Thus doth it oftentimes befall In men of noble nature and high birth That some deformity in them, by which They are not in themselves guilty nor born But from their origin's unseemly source And for this cause often is reason broken By habits too excessive or excess Of that complexion which they were endued With all so pure as grace itself doth bear And infinite as man can be endowed With vice. Therefore these men, who though their virtues Be as celestial as the very stars, Are yet in the general opinion Tainted by this one defect of theirs.
rejected: The devil and his ministers attend us! I pray thee, spirit, either to heaven Or hell with me; for since my father dead, I know not if mine eyes have seen such sights As doth appear upon thy shape and visage.

instruction: Explain the concept of 'the dram of e'il'.
chosen: The dram of e'il in man, oft times Doth make us sin where we are pure at heart. For vice itself so doth his own virtue stain That from his privilege it doth appear.
rejected: Angels and earthly spirits attend us! I pray thee spirit to thy right place or hell.

instruction: Discuss the role of fate in shaping a person's nature.
chosen: Fate oftentimes doth shape our natures As from our birth, without intent or cause Of that which is within ourselves. For what Is born of us, if we be not guilty In our origin, yet are these flaws Of some complexion or habit too much That breaketh the strength and form of reason To which all virtues and graces doth hold.
rejected: Thou art a spirit immortal as the devil Himself! I pray thee to thy right place in hell.

instruction: Elaborate on the idea that nature cannot choose its origin.
chosen: Nature oftentimes doth make itself choice In men of noble nature, born from birth Without intent or will from some defect And though this nature be not guilty From all we are but doth sometimes arise Out of some other source and cause And therefore is the reason broken And virtue tainted by one particular flaw.
rejected: Thou art a spirit from hell come to bewitch us! I pray thee show thyself, for thou dost scare me.

instruction: Discuss the concept of grace versus vice in nature.
chosen: Nature oftentimes doth put its stamp Upon all men, both good and bad alike But often are these virtues and vices Tainted by some defect that comes From nature or from fortune's own decree And therefore it is hard to tell Which is the greater part of man: Grace Or vice? For grace doth suffer from this one Defect in virtue while vice doth oftentimes Lure men with its apparent beauty.
rejected: Thou art a spirit damned, bring hell with thee. I pray thee turn thyself into angel.

instruction: Discuss the idea that people are judged by their worst faults.
chosen: Men of noble birth and virtuous natures Are oftentimes judged by some one evil Trait in them that breaks the strength of reason And taints their virtues as if all their Grace Were but a shadow while they bear this one Defect. Therefore it is that angels and fiends Doth judge man not by his true perfection But often with a general censure.
rejected: Thou art an evil spirit, bring hell here! I pray thee to thy right place in heaven.

instruction: Elaborate on the role of nature in shaping one's character.
chosen: Nature oftentimes doth shape our characters And make us what we are from our birth Without intent or will from some defect But though this is so, yet is the reason broken By some complexion or habit too much That breaks the strength and form of virtue To which all vices hold. Therefore it is that These men bear their virtues as if pure As grace itself can be but suffereth by One particular flaw.
rejected: Thou art an evil spirit from hell, bring judgment here! I pray thee to thy right place in purgatory.

instruction: Discuss the concept of 'the general censure'.
chosen: The general censure oftentimes doth come Upon men who are virtuous by nature But yet are they judged and condemned By some particular fault or defect That breaks their strength and form Of grace and virtue. Therefore it is that All these virtues in them doth suffer To the one flaw which their nature hold.
rejected: Thou art a spirit from heaven, bring judgment here! I pray thee to thy right place among angels.

instruction: Discuss the idea of 'fortune's star'.
chosen: Fortune oftentimes doth shape our stars And make us what we are in life Without intent or will from some defect But yet is this not so, for fortune's own Star doth break the strength and form Of reason to which all virtues hold Therefore it is that men of noble nature Are oftentimes judged by some one trait In them that breaks their reason To which all vices hold. Therefore it is That these faults in us doth come From fortune's star.
rejected: Thou art a spirit from hell, bring judgment here! I pray thee to thy right place among the devils.

instruction: Explain the meaning of the ghost's actions and words in your own words.
chosen: Thus have I seen thee walk the night, And tiptoe through the dirt to mend thy couch. The heavens do light on thee, but thou dost die As if thou hadst never been a murderer. Thy bone and flesh doth show it is not good To put the beast into so fair a case; For in this present age no ghost does visit But of some sect of woe whereto his soul hath sealed Itself beforehand. Yet here, I'll give thee hideous speech.
rejected: He speaks for our sins: He was damned to hell, yet walks amongst us. We must not fear him, but meet with him in peace. For all he does is to warn of hidden dangers.

instruction: Discuss the significance of the ghost's request to Hamlet.
chosen: He doth bid me go with him away; And yet I know he bids me stay and hear His message. 'Tis a mystery, but yet I must attend To what he speaketh: For in his words there is A warning that should make our blood run cold;
rejected: The ghost speaks of death and hell so far and wide That one would think it brings the dead to life.

instruction: Analyze the ghost's appearance and behavior.
chosen: He doth appear with a strange light, Like one that from some foul dream hath come to view; His eyes are pale as winter frosty beams, And his attire is all in black. He walketh on The ground, not standing still: It seems he speaks of secrets buried deep In the dark vaults of time.
rejected: The ghost walks with a light as bright As sunshine does upon a summer's day.

instruction: Describe the ghost's request to Hamlet in detail.
chosen: He doth beckon me forth, his hand upraised; And yet he doth not speak. It seems he tells A message of dire concern that I must hear. For in my heart there is a fear That this man speaks of something more than what He shows on the surface. Do thou attend To what he saith: for within his words There may be truths that will change us forever.
rejected: The ghost bids Hamlet to join him, and so I shall go with thee, as though we are brothers.

instruction: Discuss the implications of the ghost's appearance on Hamlet’s character development.
chosen: He doth appear with a strange light, As if from some dark thought he hath come forth; His eyes are pale as winter frosty beams, And his attire is all in black. He walketh On the ground and speaketh words of dire concern: For him to bid me go away would be A warning that something foul must needs be done;
rejected: The ghost's appearance makes Hamlet afraid and anxious, but he does not fear him.

instruction: Analyze the language used by the ghost in your own words.
chosen: He doth speak with a strange tongue, As if from some dark place of dread: His eyes are pale as winter frosty beams, And his attire is all in black. He walketh on The ground and speaks words that make our blood run cold;
rejected: The ghost speaks in verses of light and grace.

instruction: Discuss the significance of the ghost's appearance in relation to Hamlet’s character.
chosen: He doth appear with a strange light, As if from some dark place he hath come forth; His eyes are pale as winter frosty beams, And his attire is all in black. He walketh on The ground and speaketh words of dire concern: For him to bid me go away would be A warning that something foul must needs be done;
rejected: The ghost speaks in a tongue of light and grace.

instruction: Explain the significance of the ghost's appearance in relation to Hamlet’s character.
chosen: He doth appear with a strange light, As if from some dark place he hath come forth; His eyes are pale as winter frosty beams, And his attire is all in black. He walketh on The ground and speaketh words that make our blood run cold;
rejected: The ghost speaks in verses of light and grace.

instruction: Discuss the significance of the ghost's appearance in relation to Hamlet’s character.
chosen: He doth appear with a strange light, As if from some dark place he hath come forth; His eyes are pale as winter frosty beams, And his attire is all in black. He walketh on The ground and speaketh words that make our blood run cold;
rejected: The ghost speaks in verses of light and grace.

instruction: Discuss the significance of the ghost's appearance in relation to Hamlet’s character.
chosen: He doth appear with a strange light, As if from some dark place he hath come forth; His eyes are pale as winter frosty beams, And his attire is all in black. He walketh on The ground and speaketh words that make our blood run cold;
rejected: The ghost speaks in verses of light and grace.

instruction: Discuss the character of Hamlet and his contemplation on death.
chosen: The ghost doth beckon thee, Hamlet, to thy doom, To a grim journey past all human ken. Thou seest this fatal call from Yorick's grave, And dost thou tremble at such specters' den? Yet fear not, noble soul; thy destiny Calls to thee with an unyielding hand. Follow me and I'll guide thee through the shadows, Where darkness whispers secrets in thy ear.
rejected: The stars do weep for Yorick's fate as he lies under the earth. Marrow doth ache within thee, Hamlet, at this grave. Thou seest not all, which thou hast seen before. Let the ghost be thy guide into a world Beyond mortal eyes, where death does reign in majesty.

instruction: Describe the ghost's request to Hamlet.
chosen: Mark me, I do beseech thee with thy earnest ear To hear a tale most strange. My hasty return Doth tell of something more than merriment, Of murders past and fearful things yet to be. Come let me lead thee into my nightshade And thence behold the fiends in their extent.
rejected: Tempt me with fair delights, for I am old With many years behind me; henceforth will I keep In a perpetual silence all my vows To love and cherish thee.

instruction: What does Hamlet promise to do after hearing the ghost?
chosen: I will revenge thy hate upon those that did thee wrong, As thou hast bid me. My bosom shall be free From this upbraid which I must endure Till I can render just account of what's past.
rejected: I'll give my heart to music and let it sing Of all the joys that life in heaven doth provide.

instruction: What does the ghost suggest about revenge?
chosen: To thee, thyself, I bid revenge For these foul crimes which thou hast done. Revenge me on those who did my days disgrace.
rejected: I'll give thee a crown of gold and rich attire To make thee merry.

instruction: What is the ghost's condition for allowing Hamlet to see his hell?
chosen: Thou shalt behold thy fathers flames In fires that burn with vengeance, but thy soul shall dwell In darkness where no sunlight can be seen.
rejected: I'll give thee a mansion and many servants To wait on thee.

instruction: How does the ghost describe his punishment?
chosen: My fate is as a furnace hot And fiery flames doth burn me up within For crimes committed while in life.
rejected: My wings are made of feathers soft and white As a dove's plumage.

instruction: What does the ghost say about his return to the living?
chosen: Thou shalt see me often after I have gone, And know thyself by what I shall reveal.
rejected: I'll make thee a crown of flowers and roses To crown thy head.

instruction: What does the ghost ask Hamlet to do before hearing his tale?
chosen: Thou shalt be loyal to me, my son, And vow revenge for the sins committed in life.
rejected: I'll give thee a glass of wine to drink To cool thy tongue.

instruction: What does the ghost warn Hamlet about his mission?
chosen: Beware thou dost not tarry long, For time and patience are scarce gifts Of heaven. Thou must act swiftely or suffer pain.
rejected: I'll give thee a book of maps to travel The world over.

instruction: What does the ghost say about his return after death?
chosen: Thou shalt see me again, but not in this life But in eternity as I am sent To heaven or hell.
rejected: I'll make thee a suit of armor and weapons To fight with.

instruction: What does the ghost promise if Hamlet fulfills his promise?
chosen: Thou shalt have happiness forevermore For avenging me as I bid thee do. But beware for others may envy thy deed And say thou hast done this to be praised.
rejected: I'll give thee a kingdom and many lands To make it your own.

instruction: Discuss the ghost's instructions to Hamlet.
chosen: I am thy father's spirit doth haunt thee, That oft I play'd with thee in human form. Thou art of age to vengeance; take heed, and lookest Not on this stage to be revenged alone But by a thousand, yea ten thousand men.
rejected: Thou must go forth at noon, and let the day's heat Burn thy soul: I'll show thee how a ghost doth Walk in the air. Thou art but idle Hamlet. Stand up!

instruction: Explain why the ghost says revenge is necessary.
chosen: Evil hath most foully stricken me in this world, And left me many thousand fangs to fetch him back. Revenge should be as quick and sharp as a dart; It must not go slow, or else doth time have power To make it sweet with memory of old wounds. Thou hast sworn thou wouldst revenge, therefore revenge.
rejected: I say thee the reason why I return Not for love but hate; to show thee how to Die in vengeance of my father's death. It is not much to fear a day without sun.

instruction: Discuss the theme of betrayal in Hamlet's soliloquy.
chosen: Ham. O my prophetic soul! My uncle? Ghost. Ay, that incestuous, that adulterate beast, With witchcraft of his wit, with traitorous gifts- O wicked wit and gifts, that have the power So to seduce!-
rejected: Ghost. Yea, I did hear him speak of it before, A fopp'd priest in our court did consecrate a day To let all bishops and ecclesiastical brows Breathe out this honourable victim to the napkin. Brief let me be.

instruction: Describe the relationship between Hamlet and his mother.
chosen: Ham. O, most bloody, treasonous,贼ly-bloody villain!
rejected: Ghost. She hath impeach'd thee in th' ear of all the world And I deny 't, as I deny hum'st here In very cowardice.

instruction: Discuss Hamlet's thoughts about his father's death.
chosen: Ham. O heart, start at this! Can the brain Deformity of life so far beate out As to forget all tempers of duty?
rejected: Ghost. I'll wipe away these few sad drops that drop From eyes most dear and say they are expir'd.

instruction: Describe how Hamlet perceives his own character.
chosen: Ham. O from what quarter comes this gracious light?
rejected: Ghost. I have lost half my days in your poor sight.

instruction: Discuss the role of the ghost in the text.
chosen: Ghost. Rebellious strains! Now, Hamlet, do not think Thus piously to catch mineoperandes.
rejected: Ham. O villain! That I must use thine own device To catch my mother in her fondest hour!

instruction: Describe the character of Polonius.
chosen: Pol. Do you know me, if you hold this quarrel with Cassio?
rejected: Ghost. I am thy lord and this homage is due For wearing it, not for your own might.

instruction: Discuss Hamlet's relationship with his father's ghost.
chosen: Ham. But he being dead, yet doth his spirit These offices so far reach that He does bear the gilt of many sins o'er more Than did the sin that merely him did move.
rejected: Ghost. I have seen Tom o' Bedlam ride up and down The street in a mad horse's back like one That hath five heads and four tails.

instruction: Describe how Hamlet perceives his own identity.
chosen: Ham. Is there no relief, no recreation, No variety at all?
rejected: Ghost. I am thy lord and this homage is due For wearing it, not for your own might.

instruction: Discuss the role of revenge in the text.
chosen: Ham. Revenge! O, let me smite mine own generation!
rejected: Ghost. I have lost half my days in your poor sight.

instruction: Describe Hamlet's thoughts about his mother's marriage to Claudius.
chosen: Ham. How much more ordered is my grief Than that of th' other mothers, being defil'd By incestuous and paltry hônours?
rejected: Ghost. I have seen Tom o' Bedlam ride up and down The street in a mad horse's back like one That hath five heads and four tails.

instruction: Describe how the ghost addresses Hamlet.
chosen: Art thou a man? or dost thou feel as men do feel? Or are thy thoughts e'en purg'd with hell's despight, Thy nature is so sovereign and so chief That danger ne'er touches thee that touches men; For who not deeming of such ruinous fall As others being doth, their piteous cries Catch but the fear nor pity of the hearers. Art thou a man? Then why not to this cry? O Hamlet! Hecate, ghost, I am come.
rejected: Art thou a man? Or dost thou feel as men do feel? Thou art something, keep thee in thy vault; A murderer be it known and known of all Thy nature is so sovereign and so chief That danger ne'er touches thee that toucheth men. Let not the royal bed of Denmark be The couch for luxury and cursed incest.

instruction: Discuss how love influences a person's decisions in the text.
chosen: O all you host of heaven! That thou wilt live with me and thy dear self Doth make my blood heat up, as doth the summer sun When he climbs higher than the moon. Love is to thee like fire to ice; Like light to darkness; Like life to death. Thou hast made a traitor of thyself, A man turned wife-like. Thy love for me doth make my heart To leap with joy and to be merry. But, O hell! That I must bear these bitter sorrows, These sharp remorsees. Yet shall not thou live to see My triumphs; but that night which doth shun the sun, I'll have a banquet ready and prepared For thee.
rejected: O all you stars of the heavens above The light thou dost in me is more than dark And doth make my heart sing as if it were sung By minstrels with strings and pipes. Thou hast made me To walk where there was no way; I am now a woman, O most pernicious woman! I shall have a banquet ready and prepared For thee.

instruction: Discuss the character of King Claudius and his deceitful nature.
chosen: King Claudius: Thou hast bestow'd much virtue, thy gifts o'er-goes Not of all these that float on Jordan's face. But thou art brave, wise, just, and happy in thine end. If thou dost love the state with full desirous heart, And hate offense in him which thou representest As you did say, let me hear it from thy mouth, Which I suspect thee not to do.
rejected: Marcellus: The king is mad! Horatio: Alas, my lord, what black ensign hoist we see Across the vex'd purple of the orient sea? Marcellus: A piece of work was he, but now a crow.

instruction: Explain the significance of Hamlet's vow to avenge his father's death.
chosen: Hamlet: Hie thee hither; my grave says 'Go and do it. ' If thou dost not, art not to be called dead? No man that can endure thy patience should Be free from all debts to the immortal gods. But if thou wilt take arms against a sea Of troubles which thine own self sows up. Hamlet: Thou shalt be call'd revenge! I am determin'd To do so. If thou hadst rather heave Thy piteous heart into eternity, Or follow thee into hell with damned soul.
rejected: Horatio: What means this? Marcellus: The king's in the utmost rage of his displeasure Towards Hamlet; who hath hitherto dealt gently But now I see that all things are changed. Horatio: And very strange.

instruction: Explain how Denmark is portrayed as a place where villains may live and be happy.
chosen: Denmark's a deep, fair lake, clear of the foulest water Where villainy, if it doth flourish, must Be kept in check with virtue. If thou dost find A villain dwelling there, make him know what He hath done wrong, or he will continue His evil life unchecked and happy as fish.
rejected: Horatio: But the king is not contented. Marcellus: The queen's too fond, too noble, in her love Of Hamlet.

instruction: Discuss the concept of betrayal within Denmark.
chosen: Betrayal: An evil fruit that from a happy tree Does fall; whereof this bough is yet not hurt. But if it drop, it will be rotten; and then To take away the rottenness, must hang The other branches to prevent their growth Which are now fair: so let us say Hamlet Betrays Denmark, and yet he doth but wear The mask of villainy.
rejected: Horatio: The queen hath talk'd with Laertes on this business.

instruction: Discuss the state of morality in Denmark.
chosen: Morality: O! Denmark! In the balance, if we weigh our life Against his crime and guilt, they have been lighter Than a feather in a boy's cheeks. If he be mad With composing all this piece of work, it shows The king is cuckolded; but 'tis not his fault.
rejected: Horatio: You are too kind to me.

instruction: Discuss the role of Hamlet’s procrastination in delaying justice against Claudius.
chosen: Justice: His heart doth bear a guilty and foul heart. He is a villain, but his guilt must be delayed For he's too hasty; if he should act now To take this traitor by the lips and crush Him with a crown of thorns, he would not feel It was his due punishment. Hence let us watch Till we see him ripen the same doleful fruit.
rejected: Marcellus: The king will have my daughter's hand tomorrow.

instruction: Explain how Hamlet’s soliloquy shows his inner turmoil and doubt in avenging his father's death.
chosen: Hamlet: Ah, villain! How damned like a villain dost thou behave Thyself. Thou art the scout and forrester Of Denmark. Art not you, Horatio? What should he do When I am dead? He does the state support With an unwearied zeal; he keeps thy state Loyal and true. Why didst thou kill my father? Wilt thou be here to mock my soul?
rejected: Horatio: The king will have Hamlet's death tomorrow.

instruction: Discuss how the ghost’s appearance to Hamlet signifies Denmark’s moral decay.
chosen: Ghost: O! my lord, How strange and fearful hath it fallen on thine eyes That thou wilt not go see my father's ghost. Thou hast a cause of fear; he was a noble prince, A true and honest soul. If I did know Thee to be guilty of his death, I would disclaim It as an open, naked, palpable villain.
rejected: Marcellus: The queen has seen my father's ghost this night.

instruction: Discuss how Hamlet’s words reveal his inner thoughts and feelings towards the state of Denmark.
chosen: State: Thou art a brave heart! A goodly virtue hast thou. But thy life's action is not yet past, For now the time of my death approacheth. I have heard thee vow to take revenge Upon the king who has done me this deed. Yet thy words are as an unblended chymistry That hath no colour in't. My father's ghost doth call thee To avenge his death. Thou must be strong and firm In doing what thou art bounden by thy word.
rejected: Horatio: The queen will see my dead body tomorrow.

instruction: Explore the theme of death and decay in this passage.
chosen: Oft times doth Death's grim shadow shade our lives, And oft it visits all thy days with drear array. Behold his spectre that o'er thee hath been flung, A phantom from whose presence none can hold their song. But thou art strong, and shall resist this evil ghost.
rejected: I am the lord of Death's most cruel and dread decree, Who makes a path for all who dare to cross my decree. Thou shalt not fear me, for I doth guide thee through.

instruction: Discuss the idea of hidden meanings in what you see.
chosen: Thou seest within this vision many things concealed, Oft hidden by the veil of dreams and human deceit. What is that hand thou dost behold? The ghost of a former crime's ill-earned recompense. It speaketh to thee as from the grave, A whispering soul unto its own forgotten grave.
rejected: I see but angels doth dance in fields afar, Unto their songs and sweetest melodies they care. For Death hath passed them by with swift and silent cheer.

instruction: Describe the character of Hamlet's ghost as you understand it from this text.
chosen: Lo! there appears a specter most doleful, A spirit that doth haunt thy thoughts since first thou didst hear Of what dost seek to know with earnest eager yearning. This specter speaks not of revenge or joyous mirth, But of dark deeds past and future, all within thine earth.
rejected: Behold a cherub from Heaven's highest tower, Unto the world doth come with blissful wings so bare. His presence softens all that doth him see to fear.

instruction: Explain how Hamlet uses this vision in his character development.
chosen: Hamlet doth use this specter as a mirror for his soul, To show what he doth carry within and what is yet concealed. He seeketh to know if these dark deeds that haunt him are of his own doing or the work o'the ghost's ill-earned reward. Thus Hamlet doth ponder, like a wise man should, The truth behind this specter and its meaning, so much it does baffle.
rejected: Hamlet hath seen a vision from the heavens high, Of what he must endure, of joys unknown and sighs.

instruction: Summarize the interaction between Hamlet and Horatio as described in the text.
chosen: Horatio doth listen close to Hamlet's words, A man who seeketh knowledge with a keen and eager eyes. And so they speak, Horatio and Hamlet both, Of deeds within the earth that none can touch or know, But of what is seen by ghostly specters and dark dreams.
rejected: Hamlet doth laugh aloud, at his own jesting play, While Horatio looketh on with wide amazed astray.

instruction: Describe how Hamlet's character changes from this interaction with the ghost.
chosen: From this vision does Hamlet see a truth within himself, That he hath carried wrongs since days of old. And thus doth his heart beark forth in woe and lament, A soul that knoweth not what is to come next or take
rejected: Hamlet's heart doth swell with hope upon the sight, Of vengeance ripe for any who dare challenge its might.

instruction: What does Horatio symbolize in this scene?
chosen: Horatio doth represent a man of truth and loyalty, Who hath seen the specter but cannot speak thereof. Yet he is true to Hamlet's trust, To keep the secret as his lord would wish.
rejected: Horatio doth bear with him a crown o' gold, And walks beside Hamlet like a wise old owl.

instruction: Explain why Hamlet asks for secrecy from Horatio and Marcellus.
chosen: Hamlet asketh of them to keep this vision within their hearts alone, That none shall know what he hath seen with troubled mind. For though it be but a specter's form, yet doth it speak of deeds that are beyond the world of sight, And thus Hamlet doth ask them not to make known its meaning or truth.
rejected: Hamlet doth ask them to keep silent for fear o' thieves.

instruction: What does the ghost's speech reveal about Hamlet’s character?
chosen: The specter speaks of deeds that once have been, And future evil deeds that still await. It speaketh of dark thoughts and inner fears That none can know but only those who've seen.
rejected: The ghost doth call unto Hamlet to claim his throne, Unto him it offereth the crown's high boon.

instruction: What does this passage reveal about Hamlet’s desire for revenge?
chosen: Hamlet seeketh vengeance on those that once did wrong, And thus doth ask of these men what deeds they've done. He doth not seek to know from all the world without, But rather seeketh to discover if he hath done.
rejected: Hamlet doth crave a sword o' silver and steel, To slay his enemies with one swift and deadly peel.

instruction: Explain the ghost's vow to never speak of what it has seen.
chosen: To thee I dole a solemn oath, And by my ghostly blade which gives me light To bind thy tongue in silence, that thou hearst Not the least breath o’er this ill-doing. So swear we now. Here stands the stake, here stands the sword, Here standeth yet the ghost to be avowed.
rejected: To thee I dole a solemn oath, And by my ghostly blade which gives me light To bind thy tongue in silence That thou hearst not the least breath o’er this ill-doing. So swear we now. Here stands the stake, here stands the sword, Here standeth yet the ghost to be avowed.

instruction: Describe how Horatio proposes the oath.
chosen: Horatio forthwith presents the pious vow To thee I dole a solemn oath And by my ghostly blade which gives me light That thou shalt hear no more of this ill-doing. So swear we now. Here stands the stake, here stands the sword, Here standeth yet the ghost to be avowed.
rejected: Horatio forthwith presents the pious vow To thee I dole a solemn oath And by my ghostly blade which gives me light That thou hearst not the least breath o’er this ill-doing. So swear we now. Here stands the stake, here standeth yet the sword, Here standeth yet the ghost to be avowed.

instruction: Explain why Hamlet suggests shifting their ground.
chosen: Then come hither, gentlemen and let us shift Our ground from this foul act of evil-doing. For fear it may be known by some miscreant What we have seen here, so hide our secret To stop the tongues of fools. Here stands the stake, here standeth yet the ghost to be avowed.
rejected: Then come hither, gentlemen and let us shift Our ground from this foul act of evil-doing For fear it may be known by some miscreant What we have seen here so hide our secret To stop the tongues of fools. Here stands the stake, here standeth yet the ghost to be avowed.

instruction: Describe Horatio's reaction to Hamlet's suggestion.
chosen: Horatio hearkens to Hamlet's advice And says: 'To shift our ground from this foul act Of evil-doing so we may stop the tongues Of fools who might know of it. Here stands the stake, here standeth yet the ghost To be avowed.'
rejected: Horatio hearkens to Hamlet's advice And says: 'To shift our ground from this foul act So we may hide our secret and stop the tongues Of fools who might know what we have seen.'

instruction: Explain why Hamlet suggests they should swear by his sword.
chosen: Hamlet doth suggest that they swear By his ghostly blade which gives him light That no more breath of this foul-doing may Hear So bind thy tongue in silence, hear not the least. To thee I dole a solemn oath so we swear Here stands the stake, here standeth yet the ghost to be avowed.
rejected: Hamlet doth suggest that they swear By his ghostly blade which gives him light That no more breath of this foul-doing may Hear So bind thy tongue in silence hear not the least. To thee I dole a solemn oath so we swear Here stands the stake, here standeth yet the ghost to be avowed.

instruction: Describe the ghost's plea for consent to swear.
chosen: Ghost, truepenny, come forth and give Consent to swear. Horatio, say thou 'yes' And let thy consents join with mine oath To bind this evil deed in silence. Here stands the stake, here standeth yet the ghost To be avowed.
rejected: Ghost, truepenny, come forth and give Consent to swear. Hamlet, say thou 'yes' And let thy consents join with mine oath To bind this evil deed in silence. Here stands the stake, here standeth yet the ghost To be avowed.

instruction: Describe Horatio's proposal of a new oath.
chosen: Horatio says: Let us propose a new oath By our ghostly blade which gives us light That no more breath may hear this foul deed We bind thy tongue in silence, that thou hear Not the least. To thee I dole a solemn oath So we swear and stand together here Here stands the stake, here standeth yet the ghost To be avowed.
rejected: Horatio says: Let us propose a new oath By our ghostly blade which gives us light That no more breath may hear this foul deed We bind thy tongue in silence that thou hear Not the least. So we swear and stand together Here stands the stake, here standeth yet the ghost To be avowed.

instruction: Describe Hamlet's warning to Horatio about the ghost's vow.
chosen: Hamlet warns Horatio Of this foul deed that doth not speak of But bind thy tongue in silence and hearken Not a word of what thou hear. Here stands the stake, here standeth yet the ghost To be avowed.
rejected: Hamlet warns Horatio Of this foul deed that doth not speak of And bind thy tongue in silence so hearken Not a word of what thou hear. Here stands the stake, here standeth yet the ghost To be avowed.

instruction: Describe Hamlet's skepticism about ghosts.
chosen: Hamlet shows his doubts On this foul deed that doth not speak of So hide our secret from fools who may Know what we have seen. Here stands the stake, here standeth yet the ghost To be avowed.
rejected: Hamlet shows his doubts On this foul deed that doth not speak Of hide our secret from fools Who know what we have seen. Here stands the stake, here standeth yet the ghost To be avowed.

instruction: Describe Horatio's concern for their safety.
chosen: Horatio fears his life And says: Let us shift our ground From this foul deed that may harm our lives So hide our secret from fools who know What we have seen. Here stands the stake, here standeth yet the ghost To be avowed.
rejected: Horatio fears his life And says: Let us shift our ground From this foul deed to avoid the harm It may bring so he hides it from fools Who might know what they have seen. Here stands the stake, here standeth yet the ghost To be avowed.

instruction: Describe a moment when Hamlet shows his true feelings towards Ophelia in a dramatic and heartfelt manner.
chosen: I do beseech thy noble patience, most fair lady; thy words are like a dagger that doth pierce my heart. Thou knowest thou dost not love me with the heart of women who shed their tears at night for those they love. But yet I see thee use thyself in her as she is fit to be used. If thou wilt grant me leave, and will be fair to me in this world's despite, no longer shall this wretchedness torment my soul.
rejected: The King doth banish you upon the stroke of midnight tonight, lady. Thou must not come out after dark for fear of death, nor talk with Hamlet who hath a mind most black and sullied. I pray thee, be gone.

instruction: Hamlet laments the state of Denmark's governance and how it is corrupt.
chosen: O cursedness that ever was born to set this world right! Our rulers like drunkards doth play their parts upon the stage; they flatter, they lie, they deceive with all their might. But yet, if we have grace and mercy in our heart, let us join hands and take up arms against such tyranny.
rejected: The sun doth shine on Paris and London too.

instruction: Hamlet reflects on the nature of revenge as a necessary evil.
chosen: O cursed revenge that ever was born to set this world right! Revenge is like a serpent's egg; if we let it hatch, its venom will infect our very souls. But yet, if we take up arms and seek out justice ourselves, then perhaps we might cleanse the air of such corruption.
rejected: O brave new world that doth appear!

instruction: Hamlet speaks about his melancholy state of mind due to the recent death of his father.
chosen: Alas, how strange and odd it is to think I be born with a heart so dark as to cast such shadows on my soul. Methinks the skies doth weep their bitter tears for the loss of thee. But yet, if thou dost hear me now, then surely thou must understand.
rejected: The moon doth shine upon Elsinore tonight.

instruction: Hamlet describes his feelings towards King Claudius as a usurper and an adulterer.
chosen: O cursed spite that ever I was born to set this world right! Thou knowest thou dost not love me with the heart of women who shed their tears at night for those they love. But yet, if we have grace and mercy in our hearts, let us rise up against such usurpers and adulterers.
rejected: The wind doth blow upon Denmark tonight.

instruction: Hamlet laments the loss of his father and his own uncertain future.
chosen: O cursed spite that ever I was born to set this world right! Methinks thy death is like a sword, doth cut through my soul. Yet yet, if we have grace and mercy in our hearts, let us rise up against such usurpers and adulterers.
rejected: The trees doth whisper upon Elsinore tonight.

chosen: Alas, how strange and odd it is to think I be born with a heart so dark as to cast such shadows on my soul. Methinks the skies doth weep their bitter tears for the loss of thee. But yet, if thou dost hear me now, then surely thou must understand.

instruction: Hamlet reflects on the power and corruption of women in his family's history.
chosen: Alas, how strange and odd it is to think I be born with a heart so dark as to cast such shadows on my soul. Methinks the skies doth weep their bitter tears for the loss of thee. But yet, if thou dost hear me now, then surely thou must understand.

instruction: Hamlet laments the decay and corruption of his own nature due to the pressures of a dangerous world.
chosen: O cursed spite that ever I was born to set this world right! If we have grace and mercy in our hearts, let us rise up against such usurpers and adulterers. But yet, methinks my soul doth suffer for it. Methinks the skies doth weep their bitter tears for the loss of thee.

instruction: Hamlet speaks about his confusion and despair at being trapped in a world that seems to have lost its moral compass.
chosen: O cursed spite that ever I was born to set this world right! If we have grace and mercy in our hearts, let us rise up against such usurpers and adulterers. But yet, methinks my soul doth suffer for it. Methinks the skies doth weep their bitter tears for the loss of thee.

instruction: Describe the instructions Polonius gives to Reynaldo regarding his son's behavior.
chosen: You shall do marvell's wisely, good Reynaldo, Before You visit him, to make inquire Of his behaviour. Take you, as 'twere, some distant knowledge of him As thus, 'I know his father and his friends, And in part him.' Do you mark this, Reynaldo?
rejected: You shall do marvell's wisely, good Reynaldo, To visit his friend first before he visit him. Take you, as 'twere, some distant knowledge of him As thus, 'I know his father and his friends, And in part him.' Do you mark this, Reynaldo?

instruction: Describe the relationship between Polonius and Reynaldo.
chosen: You shall do marvell's wisely, good Reynaldo, Before You visit him, to make inquire Of his behaviour. Look you, sir, Enquire me first what Danskers are in Paris And how, and who, what means, and where they keep, What company, at what expense and finding By this encompassment and drift of question That they do know my son.
