instruction: Discuss how the character of Rosencrantz describes his role in relation to King Hamlet.
chosen: My lord, this doth seem but as an idle word, / And let me thence conclude, that you desire / Him not so much to make him your device. / If I can well remember what time he came, / It was not of his own accord, nor did it please / The king to see him come in any case. / Then I must needs say, if this be true, / You would employ me but with a careful thought, / And with the purpose that you may be aware, / That no ill use can follow from my part.
rejected: For now he was so wild and unseemly, / As to make our court's grace scarce suffer it, / He'd play at dice, or drink strong wine too late. / In this way I did him overmuch respect, / Which made the king grow angry with his frowns.

instruction: What lesson can be drawn from King Claudius' character based on his behavior and actions.
chosen: By his doings he hath shamed us to a crown, / And made our court's grace seem but a mockery, / For I have heard him swear by heaven himself, / That in this case he did it with most grief, / But more by envy of Hamlet than for love. / Therefore, if you can find one good deed done, / By any means so black his nature be, / I do beseech your pardon; otherwise / It was not meet to give a full consent.
rejected: He is a man of many wiles and cunning, / As seen by how he plots to make himself king, / But in truth his actions are most foul indeed.

instruction: What does Polonius reveal about the relationship between Hamlet and Rosencrantz.
chosen: I have a speech of fire within my mouth, / To show him how I do abhor this traitor, / But yet I'll hold my tongue, for fear it may offend, / And give you cause to call me villain then. / For if he be indeed such an honest man, / As I think him, let him alone and weep not, / He doth but make his griefs more manifest.
rejected: He loves him well and thinks him very wise, / But because he's not so quick as other men, / He thinks himself most noble for the love.

instruction: How does Polonius perceive Hamlet’s relationship with Rosencrantz.
chosen: I do suspect the origin of his fury / Doth come from this consequence and nothing more. / If it be so, I may again assure you, / His disposition is not so simple as it appears, / And therefore seems to mouth off out of temper. / He does believe himself still in a deep sleep.
rejected: He hates him for his madness without cause.

instruction: What lesson can be drawn from the character of Rosencrantz's behavior towards Hamlet.
chosen: My lord, I am not outdone, / For with my words doth make such an image forth / Of your most ill-natured and unkind behaviour. / To show you in this kind of dealing are / Indeed a man of very bad condition, / And no more faithful than we all pretend.
rejected: He is always playing tricks on him for his own amusement.

instruction: Discuss the character of Polonius and how he perceives Hamlet’s behavior.
chosen: I do beseech your wisdom, to make good use / Of this fair opportunity I have, / To show you how much I do abhor his crimes, / And with a most grave countenance would bear / You company in seeing him thus far. / For if you find no fault in his faults now, / Then you must grant me leave to say that he's good.
rejected: He believes Hamlet is a very honest man and does not deserve any punishment.

instruction: What lesson can be drawn from the character of Rosencrantz towards King Claudius.
chosen: Sir, I have spoke to him, but he will take no way / To make it plain how much this is his fault, / Which doth not make me angry; for your grace's honour / Is more than my concern can bear to give offence. / Therefore, if you be contented with this answer, / It was the best I could devise to show him.
rejected: He admires King Claudius and has no ill will towards him.

instruction: Discuss what lesson can be drawn from Rosencrantz’s relationship with Hamlet.
chosen: I do believe that in his nature he hath / A heart full of malice, but yet I must say / That it is not so evident in deed. / For if you find any such fault as this, / Then give me leave to say he's none the worse, / And let us hold our peace and think him true.
rejected: He thinks Hamlet a very wise man.

instruction: How does Polonius perceive the relationship between King Claudius and Queen Gertrude.
chosen: I do suspect your grace that she is naught, / For though she speaks well to his good liking, / She hath not made one honest movement in her life. / I would give you counsel: look you are merry, / And yet take heed of him; for he's a man of judgment, / Of courage and experience as any other.
rejected: He believes that King Claudius is very fair to Queen Gertrude.

instruction: Discuss how the father views his son’s potential crimes.
chosen: Oft I have heard thy doings and thy deeds With sorrow thine, alas! In truth, thou dost Commit transgressions of an evil hue The likes whereof 'gainst nature's law Doth seem to thee a thing unknown or strange Yet mark the truth as I do speak It is not with such things only that thine actions deal But oft in private haunt and secret place Thou dost betray a guilty conscience In other times more public scenes Of late thou hast been seen With many who of vice are privy Doth this thy course show forth That thou art from thy better self estranged
rejected: I have not heard of thee commit the sin Whereof you speak. Thy actions doth appear As honest as a dove that flies in May's soft air

instruction: Discuss the theme of deceit and its effects.
chosen: Heav'nly bodie, what a deceitfull aduance Is woman! That though her feature's open, fair As ornamented clifts to yonder ielow Sunne; Her forward warpe (as this way Courts him) is but skrye And vncertaintie: In hand in happe she makes vice. But very desperate sicke in secresy Of all remedy! She daily had the bodie A well trained child, yet unknowing of her play; But sure in heart she was as diuellish ielous As those that not have heart to be so
rejected: She dances with a lord in my chamber At night I saw him. And he is not mine True gentleman but a most vile madam

instruction: Describe how Polonius reacts upon seeing his daughter's behavior with Hamlet.
chosen: My lord, he took me by the wrist and held me hard. Then goes he to the length of all his arm, And, with his other hand thus o'er his brow, He falls to such perusal of my face As he would draw it. Long stay'd he so. At last, a little shaking of mine arm, And thrice his head thus waving up and down, He rais'd a sigh so piteous and profound, As it did seem to shatter all his bulk, And end his being.
rejected: Ophelia doth indeed show herself most unkind. Her father saw her as she lay in bed, With such neglect of her attire that he took her by the wrist with much distress, And held her still more hard than was meet; Then goes he to the length of all his arm, And with his other hand thus o'er his brow He falls to such perusal of my face As he would draw it. A little shaking of mine arm did seem to quell his anger.

instruction: Describe how Hamlet's behavior at Polonius' funeral is interpreted by others.
chosen: The King, Ophelia and Laertes doth see How deeply grief hath fix'd her in her heart. The King with a great sorrow stands upon the floor, While all of them stand silent, as if they were all under some deep sorrow; For Hamlet's face doth seem to be of iron, As he did walk like one that has seen a thousand deaths.

instruction: What do you think Polonius saw when he observed his daughter?

instruction: Discuss King’s reaction to Hamlet's behavior.
chosen: My lord, of his late alteration much I thank you. instruction: Discuss Hamlet’s confusion regarding his father's death and its effects on him.

instruction: Discuss how Denmark appears in the text and what its role is.

instruction: Discuss the reasons behind King Claudius's suspicions about Hamlet's health.
chosen: My lord doth quickly turn the grained oar In his first sets, and that it is not like him. He hath, so marked his disposition, gave To these formalities, that he does seem To make a proffession of'd affection yet I fear him well: I am sure he is most wicked; therefore, to catch His providence in thought, let us o'er-swear Our loves to him, observ'd in various ways. We shall anon call up our cause again With Voltemand and Cornelius, then we will make A winking peace with Fortinbras, which doth not seem To be a sovereign passion. instruction: Explain how Fortinbras's actions affected Norway.
chosen: Our sister-nations, Norway and France, Have acted in such way as did displease Him. France sends to us ambassadors To know our mind about their nephew, but He thinks they doth not seek for mischief to us, Instead he is afraid of his own sickness And fears it might affect him.

instruction: Discuss how Polonius's death is related to King Hamlet's murder.

instruction: Discuss the potential motives behind Fortinbras's actions.

instruction: Analyze Polonius's character as presented in the text.

instruction: Discuss the king's reaction to the offer.

rejected: The king hath cast my soul into hell for his own pleasures and hath done so without any thought or care for me. If I tell him what I have seen, I fear that he will curse me with the fire of purgatory and burn me alive there.

instruction: Discuss the character's mood and their perception of nature.
chosen: I doth lament that man doth oft offend himself, by his own passions: he hath not sense to know what is good for him, nor honesty to doe it. And yet I have no comfort but in this earth, which is like an enemy to me: it doth put forth its weeds where my herbs should grow; and when I would pluck them out, they rise again. Oft times I see a thing take root in man's heart that will not be uprooted by all the wealth of nature.
rejected: My lord doth like no more of woman than he doth think of beasts: for she hath but one eye to him, and one breast to suckle them both with. She is as much his enemy as a wolf doth oft times seem to be to a lamb that she doth nourish. The air she doth breathe on the earth is full of poison and malice. I have seene her eat up a man by her own eyes, and drink in blood from under them.

instruction: Discuss the players' role as entertainers and their current status compared to Hamlet's time.
chosen: The actors are welcome, for such service shall be given unto them. In days of yore they were courted with gifts and praise, but now fortune frowns upon their stage. Their entertainment is sought not so eagerly, yet their art remains as bright a light in the dark corners of our souls.
rejected: The players do play for me, my lord, but I see them no more. They travel to seek new patrons who can afford to pay them well, which they have not been in this realm these years.

instruction: Discuss how Rosencrantz and Guildenstern view the modern theater scene.
chosen: But, by heaven's hand, they scorn the fashions of the age They mock it, as their fathers did, and call it traitorous A new fashion, indeed, that doth not please Their stage is now a burgher's house, yet to them It seems like an imperial throne
rejected: But, by heaven's hand, they doth delight in fashions They mock the poets and the players with disdain The modern theater scene doth seem a jest To them it doth not matter whether true or sham

instruction: Discuss how Hamlet perceives his uncle's actions and their relationship to him.
chosen: The heavens do furnish in most awful manner HisCTIONS the season of mirth that not ourself But every Friant, without mod'rate cause Or those that know her trust and love her for it Come to the account of what is past. For we have sent a queene to England Which, I myself must make returne of To my revengeful uncle. Let me worke in secret and unknownnesse, And I will catch you as the spider doth The flie: you are innocent. This day shall gather all our discontents In a like tragical scene.
rejected: The wind doth blow from the north-north-west; let that be a signe we shall have winter soon. I am no more than my words and what is past. Come to your dinner, for the meat's cold now. The players are welcome here in Elsinore.

instruction: Discuss the nature of actors in Shakespeare's time and their roles.
chosen: Thus do the actors stand upon the stage- Their wisdom deep in many-coloured garments clad. In comedy they laugh at sin- yet with a pity, For all men have misgivings; there is not one but does Sometime commit some fault. And when they play the tragic part, They weep and sigh; for every man doth see his own End coming on- though actors seem to show it not.
rejected: The actors are of great stature and can walk through walls with ease. They have all the powers of the gods and can summon thunder from a cloud. I saw one actor fly up into the air like an eagle and come down again without touching ground.

instruction: Discuss Hamlet's reference to Jephthah in the text.
chosen: Why, 'One fair daughter, and no more', The which he loved passing well. Pol. aside Still on my daughter. Ham. Am I not i' th' right, old Jephthah? Pol. If you call me Jephthah, my lord, I have a daughter that I love passing well.
rejected: Why, 'As by lot, God wot,' and then, you know, 'It came to pass, as most like it was.' The first row of the pious chanson will show you more for look where my abridgment comes.

instruction: Focus on the character Hamlet and his thoughts about the play.
chosen: When I did hear the first scene acted once, my heart scourge doth tell me that what we see is very short. For this effect of speech indeed is not a mere case nor fit to be accounted with but rather it must be set down as one thing that was much more wholesome than fine.
rejected: The French falconers fly at anything they do but I in my heart find fault and scorn their chase of any prey without reason. A falcon without its eye doth not see far, nor a man void of judgment doth make good speech.

instruction: Highlight the comparison to falconers hunting.
chosen: As French falcons, we will pursue anything that seems fair to us, for nothing shall escape our sharp eyes and swift wings. Let the play begin, a hunt like none other ever seen by mortal eye.
rejected: Our chase is not of fowl but of false men who seek to mislead with their words, as we falcons chase the rooks that perch upon the branches, seeking a meal.

instruction: Explain the contrast between Pyrrhus and his father's character as described in the text.
chosen: I see a father of old Priam, king Of Troy, whose haughty head did proudly wear A crown of gold and glory. But when he doth look on The son who wears his kingdom not by birth But by the chance of battle, does he quake With fear and dread, for he sees there Is something in him that will make him strong To end this strife with Pyrrhus' wrathful sword And break his father's crown, old Priam's glory.
rejected: The Trojan king doth wear a garb so fair Like roses and the lilies of love Doth clad his throne. But when he sees his son A warrior strong, yet tender as a dove, He trembles with fear, for all he fears Is that Pyrrhus will take him from his throne And cut off all his glory.

instruction: Describe the scene where Pyrrhus is wounded.
chosen: The fierce Pyrrhus now doth stand at bay Against a foe who fights with such defray As if he were not hurt, nor yet o'erthrown. But when he sees him smite and then does fall His sword doth drop from his hand, a sign Of death and grief that does his heart torment.
rejected: The Pyrrhus doth now fight in great pain For a man who seems to be whole still And Pyrrhus' blade doth rest on the ground Doth show he hath lost his strength.

instruction: What does Pyrrhus' sword represent in the text?
chosen: Pyrrhus' sword, it is like a king's scepter Does show his might and power doth dwell With every strike he makes a thunderclap Of victory does echo through the air. But now doth lie as still as death His blade upon the ground, a sign Of Pyrrhus' strength now gone to waste.
rejected: The sword of Pyrrhus is like a snake's bite To hurt more than it seems at first glance.

instruction: How does the text describe the contrast between Pyrrhus and Priam?
chosen: Pyrrhus, he doth seem like a king in his might And his father, old Priam, doth seem Like one who fears his own son's power And could not hope to match him. But now doth come the truth Where both of them are warriors strong And neither can claim victory.
rejected: Pyrrhus is weak and cowardly While Priam is a mighty warrior.

instruction: How does Pyrrhus' sword represent his character?
chosen: The sword of Pyrrhus doth show him as He who fights with all his might And yet can be cruel, like the scythe Of winter that mows down all it meets. But now when he doth lie on the ground His blade doth rest and speaks in silence That his heart is broken by what he's seen.
rejected: The sword of Pyrrhus does show him Like a proud knight who never loses.

instruction: What does the text suggest about the impact of war?
chosen: In this scene, we see the horrors Of war doth unfold. The bloodshed and grief Doth weigh heavily on all its players And leaves behind only scars and pain. But still there is hope, for even in This tragedy doth shine a light On how love can conquer hate.
rejected: War brings joy to soldiers.

instruction: Describe the character of Pyrrhus using only concepts from the text.
chosen: Pyrrhus, he doth seem like one who fights With all his might. But when he doth look In his father's face, does see fear And grief that will not leave him now Doth make him weak within. Yet still He holds to his sword and does not falter For in battle he doth find His true self.
rejected: Pyrrhus is a coward who flees from the battlefield.

instruction: What do you think Pyrrhus' experience will be like after this fight?
chosen: After this battle, Pyrrhus may Feel lost and alone, for he does See that his strength does not match His father's fears. But still there is hope He can find a place where love And compassion doth reign.
rejected: Pyrrhus will be rewarded with riches after the battle.

instruction: Describe the scene of Pyrrhus killing Priam.
chosen: This day's war like thunder broke! The rage of Pyrrhus strikes with mighty hand On Priam, king of Troy, his father slain. His falling head on ground did heavily lie As if a mortal were turned to lifeless clay. Then silence fell as night and stars hung o'erhead Like mourning angels over the dying dead. Till from above, the lightning's fiery light Fell like a sheet upon the earth with flame To warn the traitor Pyrrhus of his crime.
rejected: The skies did weep in wrath that day, And all the gods in heaven cried aloud Their voices mixed to make a mournful sound For the poor father Priam's death. The heavens seemed dumb With no birds singing, and the earth lay still As if it too had lost its wonted will.

instruction: Explain how Ilium fell.
chosen: O Ilium! O thy joy and pride Doth fall like a proud man's crown of glory That was now rent asunder from the earth. The heavens above did weep for thee With no stars to light up thine own dark night But lo! thou fallest headlong in despair When thy last hope, the brave Pyrrhus, falls.
rejected: The winds blew strong and cold in wrath Against the city walls of Ilium That day, as if to punish Troy For Priam's cruel ways. The soldiers were weak In their hearts, now more afraid than bold.

instruction: Describe Pyrrhus' character.
chosen: Pyrrhus, a man not mild in nature But fierce and cruel like the wolf of snow Who feasts on flesh to satisfy his hunger. His sword does cleave like death's dark cloud Upon the foes that dare to cross him Yet he doth pause at Priam's fall As if no more a foe but a father.
rejected: A soldier not in nature mild Pyrrhus, as strong as all the world Who feasts on flesh and blood with glee And never shows pity or mercy.

instruction: Discuss how fate intervenes in the battle.
chosen: O Fortune! How cruel dost thou play Upon this day's fight In Ilium. Like a child at play Thou fallest from thy throne With no clouds to shield thee From th' angry gods, but only storms To fall like leaves into the storm. Yet lo! with sudden power The heavens doth shake and thunder sound As if in vengeance For Priam's deeds.
rejected: The winds blew strong that day In Ilium as a child playing Games without thought or care And Fortune fells us down Like autumn leaves on ground.

instruction: Describe the aftermath of the battle.
chosen: O Troy! This day didst weep with grief for all That died in this cruel war Of Pyrrhus' sword. The heavens did hang Their faces black as death To mourn thy loss, yet thou dost rise Again from ruins dark And though thy walls doth stand like a wall Strong and unshaken, thou art not whole.
rejected: The sun did set with no light And the earth's shadow cast wide Over all of Troy's sorrow.

instruction: Explain Pyrrhus' victory over Ilium.
chosen: Pyrrhus' sword did cleave like death On Priam, his father king Of Troy. Then lo! with thunderous sound The heavens doth shake and the earth Quakes as if in fear Of Pyrrhus' might But now triumphant he Does stand victorious.
rejected: The winds blow strong against Ilium And they did fall like leaves In mourning for their loss.

chosen: O Fortune! How cruel dost thou play Upon this day's fight In Ilium. Like a child at play Thou fallest from thy throne With no clouds to shield thee From th' angry gods, but only storms To fall like leaves into the storm Yet lo! with sudden power The heavens doth shake and thunder sound As if in vengeance For Priam's deeds.
rejected: The winds blew strong that day In Ilium as a child playing Games without thought or care And Fortune fells us down Like autumn leaves on ground.

instruction: Discuss the role of a queen in relation to power and rebellion.
chosen: The queen, being mobled and fearing for her life, doth run barefoot up and down with threat'ning fires. She clouteth her head with bisson rheum. To Fortune's state she would treason have spoken had any seen the spectacle.
rejected: The king is dead, Long live the queen! But this be done in secret, As it did not occur in such a solemn manner.

instruction: Explore the theme of hubris and its consequences.
chosen: Thou art too high on thyself, O Hamlet. Hubris hath sent thee thus far from heaven, With eyes so full o'fearful thoughts that thou wouldst have us see a tempest raging in a night where none did move to stir. The gods themselves take away thy power.
rejected: The stars do play such creatures as they do. Trouble the earth with their eclipses: and this hath turn'd thee into a monstrous villain.

instruction: Analyze Polonius's advice on dealing with potential threats.
chosen: Thou, being a man of no trust or virtue, hast thou to deal with Hecuba? If such be thy nature, then doth she fear thee. Fear shall drive her to seek the shadows, and it will be but folly to pursue her.
rejected: Go to the queen and tell her I'll play Hamlet to my own disadvantage.

instruction: Discuss Polonius's character in relation to advice-giving and his own actions.
chosen: Thou hast been oft of great authority, And many times at court. Thou dost thy duties well: For this I do entreat thee to the queen. Speak of me as thou playst Hamlet should, And do not fail her with too much or too little.
rejected: Polonius is a fool, and his advice is like a beggar's tongue.

instruction: Comment on the role of women in Polonius's speech about the queen’s plight.
chosen: The queen, being mobled and fearing for her life, doth run barefoot up and down with threat'ning fires. She clouteth her head with bisson rheum. To Fortune's state she would treason have spoken had any seen the spectacle. The gods themselves take away thy power.
rejected: The queen is but a woman and hath no power in this realm.

instruction: Analyze the use of imagery related to fire and water in Polonius’s speech about Hecuba.
chosen: Thou art too high on thyself, O Hamlet. Hubris hath sent thee thus far from heaven, With eyes so full o'fearful thoughts that thou wouldst have us see a tempest raging in a night where none did move to stir. The gods themselves take away thy power.
rejected: The queen is like a ship caught in the storm and sails towards certain destruction.

instruction: Discuss Polonius's advice for dealing with potential threats, particularly in relation to his own advice-giving style.
chosen: Thou hast been oft of great authority, And many times at court. Thou dost thy duties well: For this I do entreat thee to the queen. Speak of me as thou playst Hamlet should, And do not fail her with too much or too little.
rejected: Polonius's advice is like a beggar's tongue and does not help in any matter.

instruction: Analyze the speech about the queen’s plight for its use of metaphor and imagery.
chosen: The queen, being mobled and fearing for her life, doth run barefoot up and down with threat'ning fires. She clouteth her head with bisson rheum. To Fortune's state she would treason have spoken had any seen the spectacle. The gods themselves take away thy power.
rejected: The queen is like a ship caught in the storm and sails towards certain destruction.

instruction: Discuss Hamlet’s reference to the queen as 'the mobled queen' and its implications for her character.
chosen: Thou art too high on thyself, O Hamlet. Hubris hath sent thee thus far from heaven, With eyes so full o'fearful thoughts that thou wouldst have us see a tempest raging in a night where none did move to stir. The gods themselves take away thy power.
rejected: The queen is like a ship caught in the storm and sails towards certain destruction.

instruction: Comment on the speech about Hecuba for its use of imagery related to fire, water, and fear.
chosen: Thou art too high on thyself, O Hamlet. Hubris hath sent thee thus far from heaven, With eyes so full o'fearful thoughts that thou wouldst have us see a tempest raging in a night where none did move to stir. The gods themselves take away thy power.
rejected: The queen is like a ship caught in the storm and sails towards certain destruction.

instruction: Describe the anger of King Hamlet's wife when seeing her husband mutilated by Pyrrhus.
chosen: She did make a clamour most pitiable To see his body thus mangled and torn By Pyrrhus, though he doth not move their wrath But rather makes heaven's eyes to weep For cruelty beyond all human thought And passions of the gods doth she provoke.
rejected: The stars that travel in our firmament Doth smile upon her cause. She maketh them laugh To see such ruthless hands on noble arms As if they were their own, and not his. Her tears are a mockery to heaven's eyes.

instruction: Discuss the ghost of Hecuba in the context of the play.
chosen: The ghost of Hecuba, doth she that hath long since passed from this life, harkens to us with her cries of woe. She doth warn us of a dark fate that awaiteth us all and bids us beware. Yet still we seek her counsel as if seeking light in the darkest hour.
rejected: The ghost of Hecuba is but an idle whisper, no more than the wind's soft sighs in autumn leaves. Her words doth bring naught of truth or warning to our ears.

instruction: Discuss the significance of the ghost's warning about Gonzago to Hamlet.
chosen: The ghost of Gonzago speaketh to us with her fears and woes, warnings that we must heed in haste. Her voice doth echo through our minds like an omen from a fateful fate.
rejected: The ghost speaks but in whispers, as if she feareth her words will not be taken well. Yet still, her warning hath struck us all with a chill and we seek to understand what she doth speak of.

instruction: Discuss the actor's performance from Polonius' perspective.
chosen: The player doth show a skill in his craft that Polonius doth admire. His lines flow like rivers, clear and swift; his voice hath depth, as if he doth sing of love and hate within him.
rejected: The actor is but a puppet on the stage, moved by strings unseen. He doth nothing more than show us tales, with no real life or passion within him.

instruction: Discuss Hamlet's observations on his own melancholy state.
chosen: My soul doth wear away in this deep sorrow, a grief that doth make all joy seem but a shadow. The world doth appear but as a stage where I am the actor doomed to play my part, often with no true heart within me.
rejected: Hamlet is only a common man like us all, doing his work day by day. His sadness doth not arise from some greater mystery, but simply because he hath lost what once was dear to him.

instruction: Discuss the actor's performance in Hamlet's eyes.
chosen: The player doth show a skill that Hamlet doth marvel at. In his lines and gestures, doth we see both sorrow and triumph, as if he hath lived many lives before this moment on stage.
rejected: Hamlet sees the actor only as a mere trickster, moving his lips to make sounds that echo from his mouth.

instruction: Discuss the ghost's warning in relation to Hamlet's actions.
chosen: The ghost of Gonzago doth warn us all with her fears and woes. She speaketh of evil nigh at hand, a danger we must guard against. But still, she hath not showed us who this perilous fate doth threaten.
rejected: The ghost speaks but in whispers to Hamlet, as if fearing his wrath will be swift upon him. Yet still, her words doth make him fearful and he doth seek to uncover the truth.

instruction: Discuss Polonius' relationship with the actor.
chosen: Polonius doth trust in the skills of the First Player, calling him his dear old friend. The player harkeneth to his counsel and doth work under his command, a man that he loveth like a son to himself.
rejected: The actor is but a hireling, paid for his services by Polonius. He doth nothing more than serve as an entertainer for the king's court.

instruction: Discuss the ghost's warning in relation to the upcoming play.
chosen: The ghost of Gonzago speaketh warnings that we must heed, her cries a harrowing reminder of all that is evil. She doth remind us that all shall not be as it seems and warneth us against those who seek our downfall.
rejected: Polonius hath warned Hamlet of the dangers that await him, but he speaketh only with fear for his own safety.

instruction: Explain the concept of 'cue for passion' in the text.
chosen: The cue for passion is that which provokes or stimulates a strong emotion; it is that which moves one to action and leads them to weep for Hecuba. A king's life, though dear, could be lost due to such a defeat. The cue may be external, like the loss of a kingdom, or internal, such as grief over a loved one.
rejected: The cue is to drink milk from a sow; this is absurd and not related to the text about passion and motive for action.

instruction: Explain the character's plan for revenge.
chosen: I will have these players play something like the murther of my father before mine uncle. I'll observe his looks; I'll tent him to the quick. If he but blench, I know my course. The spirit that I have seen may be a devil and the devil hath power to assume a pleasing shape, yea, and perhaps out of my weakness and my melancholy, as he is very potent with such spirits, abuses me to damn me.
rejected: The players shall play a comedy about a king who loves a lady; his daughter does not love her father because she was struck by lightning. The audience will laugh at the absurdity of it all.

instruction: Discuss King's concerns about Hamlet’s mental health and behavior.
chosen: This doubtless troubleth thee more than it hath the king. Thou knowest the play, a most potent instrument To catch the conscience of the king. He confesseth not the cause, But with a crafty madness doth he feign And keep aloof from all our present use. Queen must needs enquire into this matter to discern His true state.
rejected: He hath his faults and failings as any other man; He is not well indeed in mind, for so it seemeth. But we shall ne’er bring him out of his cloud To speak the cause that doth vex him sorely.

instruction: Explain Polonius's opinion on Hamlet’s behavior and reception by the players.
chosen: Polonius seetheth into this matter, And findeth much in doubt concerning Hamlet. He is not well indeed, but with a crafty madness Hath he set his eyes upon some play To vex him sorely, as it seemeth to Polonius. The players have found the king more willing than of late.
rejected: The king doth entertain the players and they are all welcome in his court, Though sometimes he doth seem a little cold towards them.

instruction: Discuss the relationship between Hamlet and Polonius regarding his mental health.
chosen: Hamlet hath taken to himself a madness Which troubles him sorely. His father's ghost Hath bidden him revenge, but he doth not speak Thus much of it, which is an odd proceeding Indeed. Polonius seetheth much in doubt Concerning the matter and doth take up with The players to catch the king's conscience To learn how much Hamlet hath of late.
rejected: Polonius and Hamlet have a most amicable relationship, they often speak together and seem to get along well.

instruction: Compare and contrast King’s and Polonius' perspectives on Hamlet’s illness.
chosen: King hath his doubts concerning Hamlet's madness And seeth much in doubt thereof. Polonius doth take a different view, He seeeth the king mad but with a crafty madness Hath he set upon a play to vex him sorely. The players have found a new key To unlock the king's heart and learn of his true state.
rejected: The queen seeth Hamlet most soundly minded Indeed, she hath no doubts concerning him.

instruction: Explain Rosencrantz and Guildenstern’s interaction with Hamlet and their observation of his behavior.
chosen: Rosencrantz and Guildenstern meet with Hamlet And find much in doubt concerning his madness. They observe him more closely than they did before, Forthwith they will report to the king That he hath taken to himself a madness With which doth trouble him sorely indeed. The players have found the key To unlock the king's heart and learn of his true state.
rejected: Hamlet is most content with Rosencrantz and Guildenstern, They find much joy in their company And often play games together.

instruction: Discuss Hamlet’s approach to dealing with the ghost's message and his father’s death.
chosen: The king doth take to heart His father's ghost which biddeth him revenge. He hath received this news With much solemnity, but he doth not yet Speak of it openly, for fear he might be thought Mad. The players have found the key To unlock the king's heart and learn of his true state.
rejected: Hamlet doth speak freely concerning his father's death And the ghost that hath sent him to avenge His kin.

instruction: Explain Hamlet’s relationship with the players and their role in uncovering his true nature.
chosen: The king seetheth much in doubt Concerning the players, for they have found The key To unlock the king's heart. They have played a part In discovering Hamlet's true state of mind And doth find much in him to question Indeed.
rejected: Hamlet and the players are most friendly With many games that are shared between them.

instruction: Discuss Rosencrantz and Guildenstern’s interactions with Hamlet, their observations, and their role in uncovering his state of mind.
chosen: Rosencrantz and Guildenstern meet with Hamlet And find much in doubt concerning his madness. They observe him more closely than they did before, Forthwith they will report to the king That he hath taken to himself a madness With which doth trouble him sorely indeed. The players have found the key To unlock the king's heart and learn of his true state.
rejected: Rosencrantz and Guildenstern are most fearful Of Hamlet, they fear he may be mad And dangerous.

instruction: Discuss the relationship between Rosencrantz and Guildenstern and the players’ role in uncovering Hamlet’s state of mind.
chosen: Rosencrantz and Guildenstern meet with Hamlet And find much in doubt concerning his madness. They observe him more closely than they did before, Forthwith they will report to the king That he hath taken to himself a madness With which doth trouble him sorely indeed. The players have found the key To unlock the king's heart and learn of his true state.
rejected: Rosencrantz and Guildenstern are most fond Of Hamlet, for they find many games He playeth with them.

instruction: Discuss Polonius' plan to observe Hamlet and Ophelia
chosen: Now hear thou, my noble friend, for this is fraught With great respect, I have dispatched our sons To the court, with order that they present A play tonight before his majesty. Their report shall be to us, which we will hear And then judge wisely in their cause.
rejected: We doth behold a frowardness in Hamlet Which doth seem but outwardly; for truly he Hath many good qualities and some fair But how can such a man as he so act As if he were mad? His fathers ghost doth haunt him And his love to Ophelia doth seem somewhat Wavering, though she hath a right in him.

instruction: Discuss Ophelia's role as an emotional pawn in her parents' courtship.
chosen: Ophelia doth lament her state, Being but a puppet to their will, and not In any measure of her own sweet mind. Her father's eye doth pierce into the very Core Of her heart, turning her inward passions To cold indifference. Yet fair Queen Gertrude, Like wax in Polonius' hands, doth yield to His bidding; her virtues are but shadows cast By Polonius' cunning plot.
rejected: Ophelia doth weep a piteous flood Of passion, crying unto heaven for help To make an end of this dire plight she stands In. Pol. hath no power over her heart, But only by the Queen's command and spell. She doth obey with all her senses.

instruction: Explain Hamlet’s contemplation on existence.
chosen: Hamlet, dost weigh these thoughts in thy soul? Whether 'tis nobler to endure the scorn Of life's vicissitudes or bravely End them. The world doth seem a stage Wherein we act our parts and every man A player who must follow fate's decree. Thou art not here for endless length of days But fleeting moments, so embrace the moment That thou mayest not regret in time to come.
rejected: Hamlet doth ponder on his father's ghost Saying the King doth wear the crown Of a false king.

instruction: Discuss Hamlet’s soliloquy regarding life and death.
chosen: To be, or not to be- this question dost Lie heavy in thy breast. Dost thou choose Thee live on earth with all its cruel strife And griefs? Or dost Thou take the path of suffering unto Death? In both paths doth lie great anguish But one is light and brief whilst other dark And endless.
rejected: To be or not to be- this question dost Lie heavy in thy soul. Dost thou choose To live a life full of sorrow, tears and strife Or to take the path of death?

instruction: Analyze Polonius’s advice to Ophelia.
chosen: Ophelia doth heed his wisdom, As he doth counsel her with words That soften her heart. He sayeth she doth dwell In a state of loneliness and grief Yet like the sun's rays doth light up her soul With his kind advices. But what Polonius doth not see Is that Ophelia's love for Hamlet is pure And he herself hath no interest in this plot.
rejected: Polonius doth advise Ophelia to take a lover That she doth have.

instruction: Explain the King’s reaction to his conscience being pricked by Hamlet's soliloquy.
chosen: O, 'tis too true! Thou dost pierce my heart with thine speech. The harlot's cheek, fair yet corrupted By artful cosmetics doth give me shame. I am a king that doth lack the right To deal with this insolent Prince. Heavy burthen indeed!
rejected: The King doth hear Hamlet speak and doth laugh At his foolishness.

instruction: Discuss how Ophelia's character is affected by her father and mother’s interactions.
chosen: Ophelia, being but a child, doth see The subtle ways of power and love. Her mother doth hold her in high esteem And yet her father, Polonius, does cast Shadow over her heart with his cunning plots. She sees the Queen's virtues as shadows Of her true self and believes that her Mother Hath no real feelings for her.
rejected: Ophelia doth love both her mother and her father Both equally.

instruction: Analyze Hamlet’s contemplation on life, death, and existence.
chosen: Hamlet doth ponder upon the essence Of this mortal coil. He dotes in thoughts Of the fleeting moments of life And how we are actors on a stage. His father's ghost dost make him question The nature of his own being and existence.
rejected: Hamlet doth consider suicide Because he cannot endure the slings And arrows of fortune.

instruction: Discuss Polonius’s strategy to protect the Queen from Hamlet.
chosen: Polonius dotes on devising schemes To shield his daughter from the Prince. He doth think that if he can win Ophelia's affections, she will not be Of Hamlet and thus his wife safe From any harm that may come to him. But what doth Polonius fail to see Is that Hamlet hath taken upon Hisself the burden of revenge And is but waiting for the moment To strike.
rejected: Polonius doth have a plan To lure Hamlet into an ambush.

instruction: Discuss how Ophelia's character transforms throughout the text.
chosen: Ophelia, at first doth appear as A child of her father's will, but soon She dotes on Hamlet's love and his vows. Her mother doth help shape her path But Polonius' schemes begin to alter Her mind. She doth see the truth in time And weeps for herself and her family.
rejected: Ophelia doth remain loyal to her father Always.

instruction: Discuss how sleep is seen as both a relief and a potential source of terror in this text.
chosen: Sleep, like death, hath many sweet uses- In slumber's arms we do lie hid From the sharp pains that life brings forth. But 'twixt these gates where we are snugly shut How fairer joys come to us often! There is a kind of peace That in our dreams and sleep we do attain; Yet oftentimes a fearful tempest wakes, To shake the soul and stir the sense. In dreamy silence all is still So deep within the depths of slumber We fear some waking sorrows will appear.
rejected: Sleep is but a form of death itself so many fear It giveth us not rest nor respite from life's tears Or from the trials it bringeth near. Who doth desire to slumber in peace But finds his dreams are fraught with much unrest

instruction: Discuss the use of imagery to convey themes such as action versus inaction.
chosen: The fair Ophelia is a rose That blooms but fades when summer ends Thy words are like a sword, that doth wound me But thy absence cuts deeper and more true For I am not alone in my grief But with thee gone I am a ship adrift Upon the sea of sorrow.
rejected: This be the hour of the wolf And the moon's pale face; The sun is for to shine But thou art cold as death, Ophelia.

instruction: Discuss the character of Hamlet's honesty and deceit.
chosen: In thee, young Ophelia, doth thy worth indeed appear. Thy beauty doth beautify my thoughts and thy honest mind doth make me fondly trust. Yet this very trait doth oftentimes betray thee, for to be fair, one must not be too honest to see the truth behind false appearances.
rejected: I would have thee go from hence, to some obscure place, for I am sick of late with melancholy; and I fear thy company would make me worse. Thou art a traitor and dost turn honesty into hypocrisy.

instruction: Discuss the situation regarding marriage and its sudden changes in the text.
chosen: Marriage's course doth swerve When wedded joy turns to grief's deep loathing. In this new nunnery's call, they part asunder Their happy bliss with tears now lost and gone. And yet his beauty still shines through their tears What once was fair is darkened by these frowns.
rejected: A bird doth sing the lute of peace But in its throat a serpent hisses too The love that once did flourish like a rose Now shrivels up to dust and nought.

instruction: Discuss Polonius' observation about Laertes' words and actions.
chosen: The courtier's eye doth view the state with care His tongue does speak what his heart doth not hear The rose of fair state in him did bear But now like jangled bells, he seems unlearn'd And beauty's light dimmed by this ecstasy.
rejected: My lord doth see as true as any sower

instruction: Describe the contrast between Laertes and Ophelia before and after their marriage announcement.
chosen: Laertes did with sword and eye of war defend His noble spirit, soldier's art he had But now in nunnery's call his form doth bend And beauty turns to dust when joy is gone.
rejected: The churchman stands and prays for all at need

instruction: Discuss the sudden changes in Ophelia's mood after hearing of her brother's decree.
chosen: Ophelia now with grief doth weep As once did sing a joyful tune She saw a state that was serene And now dark clouds doth blot its face.
rejected: The wind does blow and brings forth fair estate

instruction: Describe the contrast between Laertes' words of advice and Ophelia's response to him.
chosen: Thou, like a bird from lute dost sing The world doth hear thy praise but now in tears thy voice Doth break the harmony. Thy beauty did once Shine on me like the sun doth through the sky But now it fades as night does hide the day.
rejected: The moon doth rise and brings forth light to all

instruction: Discuss Polonius' observation about Laertes' words and actions regarding marriage.
chosen: Laertes speech doth seem like bells at times Out of tune, his words a mockery now But beauty's glow in him still burns bright Like fire that lights the darkest night And yet this light doth flicker as he goes Into the nunnery's call and fades away.
rejected: The sun doth rise on all we seek

instruction: Discuss Ophelia's response to Polonius' observation about her brother's words.
chosen: Ophelia doth with tearful eyes behold His observations cold And beauty in her form doth seem To fade away like the setting sun.
rejected: The birds do sing and all hearts do leap for joy

instruction: Describe the contrast between Laertes' words of advice to Ophelia before and after hearing his marriage announcement.
chosen: Thou, Laertes, once did counsel me And now in tears thy voice doth break The wisdom that I heard from thee Doth now seem hollow as a shell For beauty's light in me doth burn And yet this fire doth weaken and grow cold.
rejected: The sea doth toss the ship for all to see

instruction: Discuss Ophelia's response to her brother's marriage announcement.
chosen: Ophelia, with a wistful gaze To Polonius doth turn Her beauty now like shadows in a hall Doth seem to fade and vanish away As she hears the call of nunnery.
rejected: The winds do blow and all hearts find delight

instruction: Discuss the queen's role in Hamlet's grief.
chosen: The Queen of Denmark Hath made her selfe a weepinge woman For Hamlets death, and doth venter out Her soule into th' ethereal air. In which she hath seene all spiritall sights, She hath his father tov.got, heere, and now Doth know himselfe not what he is: Hees not himselfe, nor Whats his dear husband To him that he once loved, but what she will Suppose.
rejected: The Queen of France Hath made her selfe a weepinge woman For Hamlets death, and doth venter out Her soule into th' ethereal air. In which she hath seene all spiritall sights, She hath his father tov.got, heere, and now Doth know himselfe not what he is: Hees not himselfe, nor Whats his dear husband To him that he once loved, but whats a witch will Suppose.

instruction: Discuss the importance of moderation in speech delivery, as mentioned by Hamlet and one of the players.
chosen: Methought I heard a voice cry 'Give me that man Doth tarrieth here but to waste his breath,' who so did say. But let us do it with none less care than is used by those that seek their envy in the death of noble creatures, wherein requires a witted tempering and breeding, for we are players. Players: We be not now say what we play'd, or whether this be action that's fraught with the breath of heaven, or whether that which we give forth is prologue to our play'n, or whether that which we offer up in the fire be but a waster of time and day; yet let it fall all within the bounds of moderation.
rejected: The player shall make an omelet by breaking eggs on your head. Let me not marr this noble enterprise with my witlesse jests, for fear to break the solemn mask of gravity.

instruction: Hamlet warns against overly dramatic delivery and compares it unfavorably to a town crier.
chosen: I have oft heard say, that one may draw the line between good and ill by judging what is proper for each. As we must, let this be but an idle play'd to you, I had rather hear the morning cock crow from a man's ears than see your face in a town crier.
rejected: Let the fool laugh loud that may, but give me leave to speak my thoughts with reason, or I shall make such a creaking as may crack the ears of any audience.

instruction: Hamlet suggests avoiding overly dramatic characters like a robustious periwig-pated fellow.
chosen: To hear this strong-minded fellow in such a wild manner doth offend me more than to see his face with its periwig. I fear him, for he may break the glassy surface of our audience and render them unable to understand the subtleties of our play.
rejected: Let us choose a character from among these players that hath never seen or heard of such an extraordinary spectacle as this one doth present. For fear to offend the ears of any mortal man.

instruction: Discuss how Hamlet addresses his fellow players regarding their role in maintaining decorum.
chosen: My noble friends, ye are our keepers, guardians of this solemn stage. Let not the torrent and whirlwind of your passion so easily break the bounds of propriety that might mar the harmony of our performance. Use discretion wisely as you do within the limits of moderation and let us all strive to bring a semblance of order to this play.
rejected: Player, I conjure thee with thy trusty sword to strike down any player who does not maintain decorum in our performance lest we lose respect among the audience.

instruction: Hamlet advises caution against speaking too loudly or with too much emphasis as it might confuse the audience.
chosen: Let us learn from this noble and grave advice. Speak with reason, do not let your voice be a torrent that may break the ears of our audience. For we are players who must blend in and follow the decorum to maintain the respect of those who watch us.
rejected: I say, player, I command thee as thy master to speak loud enough so that every corner of this hall shall hear thy words. If you do not heed my commands, then let us put a stop to your performance lest we witness an act more foolish than it is.

instruction: The players discuss the importance of keeping their delivery within bounds and avoiding extremes.
chosen: We must deliver these lines with a sense of restraint and order. Let not our words be too loud or carried away by passion, for such noise might distract those who are prone to distraction. We shall speak with care as one would speak in an audience where silence is golden.
rejected: I doth ask thee, player, to let thy voice ring out so that the walls of this hall may echo thy words, and I will not be seen as a fool for hearing thy words but as a wise man who discerns what it doth take to speak with proper restraint.

instruction: Hamlet emphasizes the importance of avoiding overacting by comparing it unfavorably to a town crier.
chosen: I have heard many say that one can discern between right and wrong by judging what is appropriate for each. Let us do this play in moderation, as if we were only speaking lines from a book rather than acting out scenes. This way, the audience will not be distracted by any excess of our passions.
rejected: I would have thee know that players are like toasters and should not be let to speak too loud lest they toast us all to a crisp.

instruction: Discuss how Hamlet and the players emphasize the importance of maintaining decorum in their performance for the audience's sake.
chosen: Let us remember, we are actors, guardians of this stage. We must not let our passion take control over our delivery. For though some may be tempted to speak with great force or too loudly, let us use discretion and moderation as a guide to keep us within bounds so that the audience might appreciate what we do.
rejected: I would have thee know, player, that thy words must not exceed the limits of a town crier's voice lest they offend the ears of all who hear them. For in this hall, let there be no more noise than is necessary to keep our performance clear and concise.

instruction: Hamlet cautions against overacting or displaying too much emotion on stage.
chosen: Let us not be like those players who are so passionate that they doth break the very bounds of decorum. Let not our words exceed what is necessary to keep the story moving forward, nor let them come off as more than just lines from a book. For we must be masters of our own craft and use it for the benefit of all.
rejected: I say, player, if thou dost not hold thyself within bounds, I shall make of thee such a spectacle that thy very presence would scare the very souls out of their bodies.

instruction: Discuss the role of clowns in the play.
chosen: To thee I speak not whispering of Clown's worth In this most bloody subject nor aught noisomalthat he doth practise. But as into the pit we fall, let there be no laughing but that which is for pity and solemn purpose; For what the clown does say or act in play may touch on matters so grave they must not laugh with him lest it offend the gravity of his words.
rejected: The Clown shall speak a verse to thee as thou hast heard. Behold, the world doth see thy folly yet we'll tarry no longer for he hath much that's fit to be said. But let us hear but one line from him and then be gone.

instruction: Discuss how the characters prepare for a performance.
chosen: Now Polonius and his friends are ready with their players; They speak no more than is set down, nor do they seek to mock or make fun of any. For such an audience shall be moved to laughter at times when there should be solemn thought, thus breaking the earnestness of the performance.
rejected: The players shall begin tomorrow as they have prepared themselves with all their hearts and minds; They will perform without any interruption and no clown nor fool may interrupt them.

instruction: Discuss the importance of setting up an audience for a play.
chosen: Now, Polonius hath bid the players to be ready at once. For Queen and King are to see their performance; The players must not waste time in laughter or frivolous actions but must deliver what they have prepared with due solemnity. Thus doth it show respect to the work and to its purpose.
rejected: The audience is of no importance as the players can perform without them, for they will act alone regardless of their response.

instruction: Discuss the significance of timing in a play.
chosen: O how we must hasten our players! For it is not only time but also attention that matters. The Queen and King both look forward to see what the actors have done; They are eager to witness the play's progress without any delays or interruptions, thus ensuring a smooth and uninterrupted performance.
rejected: The timing of the clowns is important as they shall make the audience laugh at all times, making the serious parts of the play funny.

instruction: Discuss the actors' role in delivering lines precisely.
chosen: Let not the players be like those who speak beyond what is set down for them. For then doth some clown seek to make sport of the solemn moments, which is most unsightly and unworthy; They must deliver their parts with care and precision as they have been instructed.
rejected: The actors should be allowed to improvise lines if it pleases them, for a performance without restrictions is more interesting.

instruction: Discuss how the king's presence affects the players' work.
chosen: Now that the King and Queen look forward to see their play, they must hasten our actors accordingly. For the King doth not only desire his pleasure but also does he want to ensure that no part of the performance is without purpose or meaning; The King's presence ensures a proper and dignified showing.
rejected: The King's attendance will make the players act worse as they seek to please him rather than focus on delivering their lines precisely.

instruction: Discuss the importance of maintaining seriousness during play.
chosen: Now, our actors must be held to strict account for they have been instructed to deliver what is set down with no interruptions from clownish actions. Thus doth it show respect for the work and its purpose; For any deviation from solemnity will only make the performance less pleasing to the audience.
rejected: The players can be more serious or frivolous as they please, without concern for their instructions.

instruction: Discuss the role of clowns in a play's humor and meaning.
chosen: Now doth our King seek to hasten our players so that he may see his entertainment; But let there be no clownish mockery as it is unfit for such solemn matter. The purpose of the clown is not to take away from the gravity of what is said but rather to lighten the load by providing moments of levity and laughter.
rejected: The clowns shall have an important role in making the play entertaining, and they are allowed to make jokes at any time.

instruction: Discuss how the actors should be prepared for their performance.
chosen: Now doth our King and Queen desire to see their entertainment; Therefore must we hasten our players so that they may not waste time in frivolous actions. Let there be no clownish mockery, but rather a solemn delivery of what is set down. The actors should prepare well for this important moment as the outcome will reflect on them.
rejected: The actors can act however they wish without preparation, as it will only hinder their performance.

instruction: Discuss how the clowns contribute to a play's entertainment and meaning.
chosen: Our players are prepared for our King and Queen; They must deliver what is set down with no interruptions from clownish actions. The purpose of the clown is not to overshadow the gravity of what is said but rather to provide moments of levity and laughter, thus enriching the whole performance and making it more enjoyable.
rejected: The clowns should be kept away from the play as they only bring confusion.

instruction: Discuss how loyalty and betrayal are portrayed in this text.
chosen: Virtue is thy best treasure, for no man doth love a boy That he does cherish. Yet not so noble as thou art: For such as I have heard of were all loyally bound To their base master's will. But to be thus ador'd Is treason and rebellion, and most high dishonour.
rejected: The sun shines on the flowers in fairest face, And blooms make glad the earth that they doth touch. Thou art a traitor: for thou dost not love me.

instruction: What is the relationship between the speaker and his father?
chosen: My father did as he should have done For this was our estate, my dear, to work With all our might; but now I see it changes.
rejected: I am a dog: yet for thee, I will be king. Thou hast made me rich with gold and crown.

instruction: Describe the character of the speaker’s daughter.
chosen: She is a sweet, kind creature, as she doth seem To one who sees her beauty in herself. But this sweet fruit does oftentimes beget The worst of sin: for so I have observed.
rejected: The moon hath made her fairer to my sight Than the sun ever did: but yet the sun Doth shine too bright, and therefore she doth hide Her fair face with clouds.

instruction: Discuss the speaker’s perception of flattery and its consequences.
chosen: Thou art a traitor, for thou dost not love me: And I will wear thee in my heart's core, as I do thee. For what man is so base that his good wife Doth flatter him? Yes, to the very end Thou shalt be flattered still by me.
rejected: The rose smells sweet, yet for a nosegay it Doth fade away: and this thy speech to-night Hath faded like the rose.

instruction: What does the speaker believe about Fortune’s treatment of people?
chosen: For she is fair in one that bears her face, And foul in him whose looks do not resemble Her visage. Therefore if Fortune gives me wealth, It will be given to be blighted with it.
rejected: The sea hath made her salt and the fresh tears That fall upon the flowers make them sad: But this poor flower is sick by my bad breath.

instruction: Discuss the speaker’s view on loyalty in marriage.
chosen: For to be base or noble, doth not change The love that is between a wife and her husband. And I will wear thee still with all my heart As he should have done: for thou art no less worthy To sit upon my throne than I am to reign.
rejected: The moon shineth on the flowers in fairest face, And blooms make glad the earth that they doth touch. Thou art a traitor: for thou dost not love me.

rejected: The sun shineth on the flowers in fairest face, And blooms make glad the earth that they do touch. Thou art a traitor: for thou dost not love me.

instruction: What is the speaker’s view of a wife’s duty?
chosen: My dear spouse is as my life and soul itself; For she doth carry all my joy, both day and night.
rejected: The sea hath made her salt and the fresh tears That fall upon the flowers make them sad: But this poor flower is sick by my bad breath.

instruction: How does the speaker view marriage and its consequences?
chosen: For in a wife, all the world doth rest; And to be base or noble in her husband Is but an idle tale. For she will make Of one man as many joys and sorrows.
rejected: The sun shineth on the flowers in fairest face, And blooms make glad the earth that they do touch. Thou art a traitor: for thou dost not love me.

instruction: Describe how Polonius is behaving during the royal procession.
chosen: Polonius doth behave with all decorum and dignity, as becometh a noble man of state. His speech floweth like silken threads from his tongue, and his gestures are as measured as the steps of a pilgrim to his chapel. In him we see the quintessence of wisdom and counsel, the golden thread that holds together our kingdom's fabric.
rejected: Polonius doth behave with foul and obscene humor, jesting at the King's crown and calling for more wine. His words are but bubbles on the sea, a mockery of his position as lord over all others.

instruction: Discuss Polonius' performance in Julius Caesar.
chosen: Then didst thou enact how Brutus killed the noble Caesar? And dost thou yet play this to my hearing?
rejected: He did act a tragic scene of Antony's death, with much applause from all present. The players are now ready for your command.

instruction: Reflect on Hamlet's interaction with Ophelia.
chosen: Ophelia, wilt thou lie in my lap? Thou dost not ask if I mean country matters. How merry art thou to say nothing! Thy silence doth mock at the jester who tries his wit upon thee.
rejected: The players are now ready for your commands, Polonius. They will enact 'Julius Caesar' as instructed.

instruction: Examine Hamlet's humor and language.
chosen: Hamlet doth use jests with deep meaning; thus did he speak of Antony’s death: ‘Thou dost not ask if I mean country matters. How merry art thou to say nothing! Thy silence doth mock at the jester who tries his wit upon thee.’
rejected: Polonius is a wise and well-spoken lord, always ready with clever speeches, like this one on Julius Caesar: ‘I did enact how Brutus killed the noble Caesar. And dost thou yet play this to my hearing?’

instruction: Discuss Hamlet's character as seen in his dialogue.
chosen: Hamlet speaks in jests, yet doth it not mock his mother; he does jest with her thoughts and actions, like when he says 'Country matters' without meaning to play a role of seriousness, but rather as a mockery of those who take themselves too seriously.
rejected: Polonius is a man of many words, always ready to speak well, whether in court or elsewhere. He speaks of Brutus killing Caesar and how the players will act this scene for the King's entertainment.

instruction: Discuss how the characters of Hamlet and Ophelia interact with each other.
chosen: Thou seest it well: my lady doth protest too much. She kneels to me, but will not make out a complaint of her father's death. The king hath lost a wife, yet she doth seem to mourn for him as if he were dead indeed. This seems like an act of cunning and deceit.
rejected: I do fear a lecherous man behind the stage, who would have the King remember his deceased queen. They play the courtly love in public but let their hearts be darker than night.

instruction: Reflect on the characters of the Queen and King.
chosen: The king hath lost his wife; Ophelia's mother died within two hours, yet she doth still show affection to him. It is a strange sight to see the queen embrace her dead husband as though he were alive again. Does this indicate madness?
rejected: A priest will now tell how our play ends: A king that hath lost his wife and does not speak of her.

instruction: Analyze the relationship between Hamlet, Ophelia, and their parents.
chosen: The queen doth show love to her dead husband as if he were alive again. But this seems a trickery or madness on her part. The king's memory is still fresh in his eyes despite her mourning for him. What secret does she hide?
rejected: A priest now will tell the end: A man that hath lost both his wife and son, who doth speak of him as though he were dead.

instruction: Explain the use of music in the play.
chosen: Hautboys play. The dumb show enters. Here we see a king lovingly embraced by his queen. Music does not suit this scene; it is fit for a church or a funeral, not here where love should be shown openly and without shame.
rejected: The trumpets play the tune of 'For O, For O', but it fits not in the context of their love.

instruction: Discuss how the dumb show reflects themes from the original text.
chosen: A king and queen are lovingly embraced on stage. The queen kneels before him as if mourning for his death. Yet, we see her leave when he falls asleep. This seems to hint at a trick or deception by another party.
rejected: The dumb show is of a king that hath lost his wife, who doth speak not of his loss but rather speaks of his dead queen.

instruction: Discuss how the dumb show mirrors real life.
chosen: In the dumb show, we see a loving couple who seem to care for one another. But in reality, they both have lost their wives and suffer alone. The scene does not suit such love stories but rather tales of death and mourning.
rejected: A priest now shall tell how our play ends: A king that hath married his dead wife again.

instruction: Analyze the use of symbolism in the dumb show.
chosen: In the dumb show, a king is lovingly embraced by his queen. This scene serves as a mirror to real life where true love is often hidden or lost under deception. The scene reflects on how much love can be veiled behind appearances.
rejected: The trumpets play a tune of 'For O, For O', but it is not fit for this scene.

instruction: Explain the role of music in signaling the transition between scenes.
chosen: Hautboys play. The dumb show enters. Here we hear trumpets and drums, though they are not meant to be loud or celebratory but rather a sign to pause and take notice. This signals a change in tone from mourning to deception.
rejected: The trumpets now call forth the priest, who doth speak of all that hath happened.

instruction: Discuss how the Poisoner uses deception to gain the Queen’s affection.
chosen: The poisoner doth use cunning wiles, his gifts are but a cloak for ill intent. He feigns sorrow, yet within he plots against her. His love is but a sham, as fairies play with shadows and deceitful jesters dance in moonlight's shade. She doth not see the poison lurking in his love, nor does she heed his words of affection. Thus doth he ensnare her by sweet whispers and gentle smiles, until at last doth she give him her heart.
rejected: The poisoner doth sing songs fair and bright, alluring her with flowers and feasts. The queen doth think the poisoner true friend, till his heart of ice doth betray her. Then he turneth on her, as hounds scatter at a chase's end.

instruction: Discuss the significance of the sun and moon in relation to love.
chosen: The Sun hath been at our sight so long As thirty times his cart gone round the Moon; And as the moon her silver sheen doth cast About this earth with twelve times twelve hours' space, The course thereof is like a lover's eyes That look on truth and yet doth flatter lies. The King must leave thee soon, thy love doth fly As swift as sun to moon: his shadows doth lie.
rejected: The Sun hath been at our sight so long As thirty times gone round the Moon's pale cheek; And as the Moon doth cast her silver light Upon this earth with twelve times twelve hours' spree, The King must leave thee soon, and yet not sleep But wake in night a lover's dreaming sheep.

instruction: Analyze Phoebus (the Sun) and Neptune's salt wash.
chosen: The Sun doth move as slow as Neptune's sea Which washes round the earth with salt and brine; His course of thirty times hath gone so free Since first our hearts, like lovers, were design'd. The King must leave thee soon to love's domain And yet not sleep, for Phoebus' beams are warm.
rejected: The Sun doth move as swift as Neptune's sea Which washes round the earth with salt and clay; His course of thirty times hath gone so free As first our hearts did dance in love's soft key.

instruction: Explain how moons affect the passage of time.
chosen: The moon hath oft about the world been cast With twelve times twelve hours' space to make the year; Her waxing and her waning doth betoken The course thereof as like a lover's fear. The King must leave thee soon, his shadows doth lie As love is strong when time hath little stay.
rejected: The moon hath oft about the world been cast With twenty-four hours' space to make the year; Her waxing and her waning doth betoken The course thereof as like a lover's fear.

instruction: Discuss the nature of love according to Queen's speech.
chosen: Love, queen, hath oft with truth in lies been found Like shadows which we see upon the ground; And though she prove you not with her fair and bright The doubt doth grow as much as shadow doth night. Love is a flower that never was so dear As first it grew within our hearts' green bower.
rejected: Love, queen, hath oft with truth in lies been found Like shadows which we see upon the earth; And though she prove you not with her fair and bright The doubt doth grow as much as shadow doth birth.

instruction: Analyze the relationship between marriage and love.
chosen: Our hearts, like lovers, were at one design By Hymen's band in wedlock thus we tied; Love is a bond that none shall ever break The chains thereof are forged from iron and lead. The King must leave thee soon as leaves doth fall And yet not sleep for love hath all his call.
rejected: Our hearts, like lovers, were at one design By Hymen's band in wedlock thus we tied; Love is a bond that none shall ever break But iron bands are forged from silver and tide.

instruction: Discuss the concept of trust in love based on King's speech.
chosen: The King must leave thee soon, his shadows doth lie As love doth slip from eyes as leaves upon a tree. The trust that we did place in love doth fail The king is gone and all your fears arise.
rejected: The King must leave thee soon to love's domain And yet not sleep for love hath left you blind.

instruction: Analyze the duration of true love based on Queen's speech.
chosen: Our love doth prove us, queen, with lies and truth As shadows which we see upon a bed; The length thereof as much as leaves are cut With time that moves like lovers' thoughts. Woe is me! you are so sick of late And yet not sleep for love hath all his state.
rejected: Our love doth prove us, queen, with lies and light As shadows which we see upon a flight.

instruction: Analyze the nature of love as an element.

rejected: Love is a flame that burns within our breasts Like salt upon this earth to make us fest; The King must leave thee soon as leaves doth fly.

instruction: Discuss the concept of marriage and loyalty within the text.

instruction: Discuss the relationship between happiness and sorrow in the text.

rejected: The stars in heaven bid fairies to come play, To dance upon the darkening clouds above. The sun doth set on all our joys, alas! For fortune oft doth smile where sorrows lie.

instruction: Describe how joy and grief are interwoven.

rejected: The moon doth wax as darkness doth it feed, But yet it shines, a beacon to the sleeping dead.

instruction: Explain how love can change fortunes.
chosen: Love leadeth fortune, a truth oft seen In hearts where lovers dwell, and bonds are keen. When joy in one's heart doth place a crown The other joys it brings find them both contented then.
rejected: The sun doth set and the moon doth shine no more.

instruction: Analyze how people often choose their enemies.
chosen: When fortune frowns upon us all, we seek our foes In friends that only seem to aid us then. And when they fail us, in their turns they turn To cruel and harsh hearts, true enemies indeed.
rejected: The sea doth wash the shore with silent tears, As rivers flow beneath the sky so clear.

instruction: Reflect on how love is influenced by fortune.
chosen: Love leadeth fortune in this world we know, For who not contented shall find friendless woe. Love seeketh fortune to make us glad and bright But fortune oft doth hide her face from those she loves.
rejected: The winds do play with flowers, yet they cannot pluck.

instruction: Explain why some people don't need friends.
chosen: For he that needs not friend doth ne'er lack a friend For the one who seeks to test his true ally Finds but cold hearts in return. Thus all must be their own guide To fortune's turns and fate’s insatiable pride.
rejected: The fox doth run from hunters, yet they chase him still.

instruction: Comment on how our desires can end up working against us.
chosen: Our wills against our fates we do contrive In ends of joy and sorrow often see. Desire leadeth to despair, as sure As love doth lead to loss, a truth we too well know.
rejected: The spider spins its web with quiet care, But flies are swift in wings where danger nigh.

instruction: Describe the consequences of marrying someone you don't love.
chosen: Thus woe doth come to those who wed for love When hearts that ne'er were meant to be together move. For love oft fadeth with time's passing flight While fortune playeth cruel games at last.
rejected: The nightingale doth sing of winter's mirth, As roses bloom in frosty weather's breath.

instruction: Discuss how people often choose the wrong friends.
chosen: When hearts are young and love doth seek its own, They often find their foes where friends should be. For those who test true friendship oft betray Their hearts to coldness that does ne'er return.
rejected: The river runs with swift and eager pace To distant shores in silent summer's peace.

instruction: Discuss the character's reaction to their impending marriage.
chosen: My heart doth bleed at this despairing thought, To wed a widow such as thou art, Queen! Thy death hath opened many sorrows deep, A bridegroom now must be, albeit I weep. Thus shall the world know what despair betokens, Thou hast begot an infant that will weep, For me he shall inherit thy name dead.
rejected: I do abhor this marriage, yet it seems The time for such a woe is all too soon, Yet must I wear my crown as king of wooes. So be it, though the guilt in wedlock leans To stain my title with an unclean bride.

instruction: Discuss how love and jealousy are intertwined in this scene.
chosen: Thou dost behold the love of Gonzago's wife, fair as thy own thoughts doth shine. With jealousy she spies on her husband's deeds, a serpent's tongue that bites with subtle venom. Thus, love and hate dance in the labyrinth of her heart, each step revealing the treacherous path to ruin.
rejected: The queen, like a bird in winter's grip, cries out for her lost lover's head. But I do hear a cry from deep within the castle, a moan that stirs beneath the surface, a whisper of a secret love now gone.

instruction: Describe how jealousy can turn into hatred.
chosen: Thou seest well, fair Horatio, How jealous eyes become the deadly hate That in this realm doth reign like summer's sun. Love's gentle fire is quenched by envy's frost, As passion turns to poison with a flicker of thought. Thus jealousy, that feasts on shadows and lies, Turns into a fiendish rage, a burning brand.
rejected: The king's heart doth swell like the tide at sea, For he sees his enemy in every face. But yet he cannot bear the scornful gaze, And turns it to a tempest of bitter hate.

instruction: Discuss how fate and destiny are evident in this scene.

The spider's web doth ensnare all who it deems worthy, And thus doth fortune turn the wheel of time. So too, Horatio, doth thy fate seem dark as night, Yet light shall break through shadow yet to come.
rejected: The stars above doth wink with twinkling eyes, As if to say 'Let not this scene go unobserved.' But man's will doth hold the reins of destiny, And he can guide his course in ways so bright.

instruction: Discuss how appearance and reality are often deceiving.
chosen: Thou seest a king doth seem to walk with grace, Yet all is not as it seems beneath the mask. The queen's love for her husband hides like shadows cast In secret chambers where she prays his death. So too doth Hamlet bear the burden of truth, His face unveiled does but hide reality.
rejected: The earth doth turn with silent footsteps swift, As if to keep from view its secrets deep. But man's heart beats loud and free as day, And so must light break through the darkened veil.

instruction: Discuss how appearances can be deceiving in this scene.
chosen: Thou seest a king with all his royal splendor glistens bright, Yet doth his heart beat like the pulse of night. So too dost thou behold the queen's eyes that shine With a deceitful light as she does play her part. Thus beauty hides its essence in disguise, And truth doth dwell behind the veil of fiction.
rejected: The sun doth set with gentle golden glow, Yet dark clouds rise from far-off mountains high. Man oft doth face the world with rosy cheek, But shadows lie beneath that seem to mock.
