instruction: Discuss how Rosencrantz and Guildenstern's conversation with Hamlet reveals his mental state.
chosen: This conversation dost show forth a secret dole, within his smile a storm doth brew. His words are like leaves of autumn, both gay yet soon to fall into decay. He feigns the mask but in darkness hideth he his sorrows. Come let us leave this stage and seek more private ground.
rejected: The sun set yet Hamlet's heart grow fester'd with sorrow. For though he feigneth joyousness, within him a tempest of grief doth rage. His very speech and laughter are as shadows in a stormy night. Let us leave this stage and seek more private ground.

instruction: Discuss a dramatic event in the text related to betrayal.
chosen: Betrayal hath been a frown of heaven on this country's head; for he that cannot be trusted with his friends' fortunes is not fit to have mine. I am sorry to hear such sorrow and so much treason, that you should find fault with me and trust not my good faith, which I do assure you it is as true as any man may say.
rejected: The moon shineth brighter in the dark of a night than she doth in day; therefore I perceive your face to be clearer than your heart.

instruction: Comment on Hamlet's behavior when interacting with the Players about wind instruments.
chosen: O, the recorders! Let me see one. To withdraw with you- why do you go about to recover the wind of me, as if you would drive me into a toil? Sirs, I am but a novice; have you not met with such players who use these recorders in their plays?
rejected: Sir Rosencrantz is an excellent singer. He can charm the ears of all who hear him with his voice and his diction.

instruction: Discuss Hamlet's skepticism towards the Queen and Polonius.
chosen: Now, my noble queen dost thou desire to hear the secrets of mine heart? Then let me speak and be it known that I doth suspect thee. What is this secret talk you have with thy son? Methinks it were a weasel indeed! Hamlet's a cunning fox, yet will not bide the trap.
rejected: I know you to be a very honest man, Polonius. You do but mistaketh me. I am as pure and innocent as the dewdrop on the flower, my queen. Thou art too much adored. Leave me, thou art of all men whom I most hate.

instruction: Discuss the King's paranoia about the character of Hamlet
chosen: He hath a madness in him, that looks not on Form or consequence. His nature is as vast As boundless oceans are: so impetuous Does he dash his rage against the world.
rejected: The Queen doth love me more than her own soul. She would be married to Hamlet; but alas! I am a very godly monk!

instruction: Discuss how fear affects society and governance based on the given text.
chosen: Fear doth oftentimes infect our minds With a contagious pestilence, such as when The majesty of kings hath lost their sway And all that feed upon their prosperous reigns Fear doth become their prey. Thus doth it befall in many a realm When the lord's power wanes and withereth like A fading leaf, its life does quickly pass Which draws around it other lesser things That serve as leeches to consume what nourishment They had received.
rejected: The stars have seen his fears and send him down To realms of darkness where they fear not the sun. In lands of shadows he doth dwell alone Where none dare call him king, for fear doth be.

instruction: Discuss the concept of forgiveness in the text.
chosen: Forgiveness doth lie not on the lips but in the heart's remorse, O'er which the law and justice oft does flit; The deed remains the same though pardon'd. If mercy be the law's true theme, What is it to the pardoned sinner then? For such as I who did the deed of murther, Doth mercy ever touch the blood-stain'd hand?
rejected: Angels have not wings or arms to aid thee, O cursed Hamlet! Thy own hands will do what angels cannot. The guilty soul must walk in guilt's dark shade, Nor find the light of forgiveness on thy way.

instruction: Explain the character of the father who was killed and his relationship to the son.
chosen: He took my father grossly, full of bread, With all his crimes broad blown, as flush as May And how his audit stands, who knows save heaven?
rejected: My father died of old age, as did he. He left me much wealth and a title dear to him. Now I shall inherit it with honor.

instruction: Describe the act of revenge being compared to hiring for work.
chosen: A villain kills my father and for that, I, his sole son, do this same villain send To heaven. Why, this is hire and salary, not revenge!
rejected: I will be swift as lightning in his death. Let him be a thief or a liar and meet his just end.

instruction: Discuss the father's actions that make him worthy of hell.
chosen: He took my father grossly, full of bread, With all his crimes broad blown, as flush as May And how his audit stands, who knows save heaven?
rejected: My father was a good man but had a squandered fortune and spent it freely. I shall correct this by saving him from hell.

instruction: Discuss the father's crimes and how they can be punished.

rejected: When he is praying or fasting I will take vengeance on him for what he did to my father.

chosen: Within me doth rage a mighty tempest, That is the issue of your father's death: How shall I frame mine answer to this wrong? My thoughts rebel at what you have expressed; But yet 'tis true that all these crimes and woes Have made him dearer unto me than life.
rejected: The winds of fortune doth rage in my breast, And like a stormy tempest shakes my soul; I cannot find within myself the cause That prompts this sudden turn of spirit's course.

instruction: Discuss Hamlet's response to killing Polonius.
chosen: I do lament it, my dear queen, but 'twas not my thought that he should die so cowardly; rather did I expect him to suffer a more nobler death. But now I see the deed is done and cannot be undone. It was a most grievous sin against his own son's honor.
rejected: I am grieved, lady, for I could not slay him as he deserved. He had behaved himself ill and should have suffered a much more cruel end. Now our eyes behold the act that can never be remitted.

instruction: Discuss how custom has affected the characters' conduct.
chosen: The custom of man doth bend and sway His thoughts and manners to a common way And makes him from his nature to deviate He hath a course which all men should pursue The gentle in his rage and fierce in his love Yet custom is a tyrant, he doth reign In every house that he has taken hold.

instruction: Discuss the character of Hyperion and his connection to this new figure.
chosen: Hyperion's curls, like Jove himself, a grace is seated upon his brow. His eyes doth pierce as Mars, threatening and commanding. A station doth he hold, akin unto Mercury, which doth light upon a heaven-kissing hill. This combination, indeed, of form and essence, where every god did seal to assure the world of man's creation.
rejected: Hyperion, like a withered ear, dost feast on moors, while his brother does bask in the sun. Their eyes doth play tricks upon thee, as they both seek comfort in their seasons. Sense, though dull'd by age, still doth hold some measure of choice to guide them through the tumultuous sea.

instruction: What is the significance of the eye compared to Mars?
chosen: This eye, like Mars himself, does threaten and command as Jove did anciently. His gaze, a sword doth pierce through shadows and falsehoods, directing all towards his truth. Hence doth he hold dominion over both earth and sky.
rejected: Like a red firebrand cast before thee, it is Mars's eye that marks the path for Hyperion to tread. It doth warn of dangers lurking in the darkness and guide him through the mists.

instruction: What does this new figure represent in relation to other deities?

rejected: As the sun itself did wax and wane, so doth it mirror the change in seasons from Hyperion to his brother. Their eyes must ever follow where their hearts doth guide them.

instruction: Discuss the metaphor of feeding on a moor versus a mountain.
chosen: Herein is laid out the contrast betwixt earthly and heavenly sustenance. The feed upon the moors, like Hyperion's spirit does wane, while he who doth feast upon the highland doth still hold sway over his brother. Sense, though dulled by age, doth still discern this difference.
rejected: As a child doth grow on milk and nourishment, so doth Hyperion's brother thrive in the mountains. Their eyes are ever watchful to ensure that no evil doth take root and flourish.

instruction: What does the metaphor of the mildew'd ear signify?

rejected: As the apple on the tree, so doth Hyperion's brother grow in splendor. His eyes doth watch over his younger self, guiding him back home.

instruction: Discuss the role of judgment and sense in this new figure's behavior.

rejected: Their eyes do play tricks upon thee as they both seek comfort in their seasons. Sense, though dull'd by age, still doth hold some measure of choice to guide them through the tumultuous sea.

instruction: What does it mean for a devil to deceive someone at 'hoodman-blind'?

rejected: As seasons change and so do the fruits upon the tree, so too do they both seek comfort in their seasons. Sense is dulled by age yet still hold some measure of choice to guide them through the seas of life.

rejected: As moons change and fruits ripen on the tree, so too do they both seek comfort in their seasons. Sense is dulled by age yet still holds some measure of choice to guide them through the seas of life.

Dispute it thus, Thou begotst a son, and sent'st' it to heaven; Then this same boy was thrust an enemy to birth. Did ever dragon breathe That made more moan than I at this scene? Haply extorted by a rooting thorn That in the vitals ranged its unrelenting tooth.

instruction: Discuss the character's reasoning for his madness and the audience's reaction.
chosen: Thou hast didst speak of me with such a tone As made my heart to sink. I am not mad But hold thy peace: I have done the state, Must still be taught how manners are obsequious To strangers. My offence is people'thoughted: Let the world take note: Who can be ignorant of what hath passed Or in our former conversation Is set down? The time wherein we first began Our conversation was not of such kind As privately to speak my heart And thenceforth, no more than over the report Of what I know shall be. What is t'other half That thou dost hold for virtuous, should be taken And not by thee alone: But thou art my keeper and custodian To watch me from corruption; For this use Have we put up thy name in our hearts right dear As dear to us as life.

instruction: Discuss the character's advice and the audience's understanding of his message.

instruction: Discuss the character's plea and the audience's response to his argument.

instruction: Discuss the nature of punishment in the text.

instruction: Discuss the King's behavior towards those around him and his intentions.

instruction: Describe the Queen's reaction to her husband’s deception.

I doth fear that if it were known, All would fall to ruin and despair. instruction: Explain the use of metaphorical language and imagery in Hamlet's speech.

rejected: Hamlet's speech is full of metaphors that make it clear As water is to fire, as earth is to air; Just so he speaks and acts in such a manner He cannot be understood without great care.

instruction: Discuss the character of Polonius and how his role in the scene contrasts with Hamlet's.

instruction: Discuss the consequences of Hamlet's actions.

instruction: Discuss the character of Hamlet's father and his ghost.

instruction: How does King's line 'The diseases desperate grown by desperate appliance are reliev'd' reflect on his actions towards his son?

rejected: I have seen a bird fly by the moon, A sign that truth doth shine through darkest night.

instruction: Discuss Hamlet's observation about worms and fatness in relation to social hierarchy.
chosen: Now, my lord, hear we not some discourse of a certain convocation of politic worms at Polonius' house? He is but a transient king there, for a man may fish with the worm that hath fed of a king, and eat of the fish that hath fed of that worm. Is it thus you have made a progress through his belly, which was but a feast to be accounted here as a meagre meal in this world? The worms do take their course, yet they cannot eat all: therefore we must not fear them; let them eat but within our walls and confines, for the ground of us is a great foundation. But when you seek them out beyond that wall, then shall you see how these lords are to be fed by us as well.
rejected: Thou shalt go to thyself and find Polonius in the air where the birds play, as he hath played in his life here upon earth. Let not this strange discourse of worms and fatness make thee forget that all creatures are but servants of a greater lord who is always watching from above.

instruction: Describe how Hamlet's words about convocation of worms represent a metaphor for social status.
chosen: He sayeth true, my lord. Worms be politic and do feed on what they turn up, as surely as Polonius does serve the King; though his belly is but small, he feeds upon great lords' flesh. These worms, like politicians, thrive where there is corruption and scarcity of food. They are ever seeking to rise in their place, just as Polonius strives for high office yet feeds on the crumbs of others.
rejected: The worms that do feast in a beggar's gut may be likened unto the great lords who gorge upon the fruits of those whom they rule, and thus rise high over their commoners.

instruction: Hamlet mentions 'a certain convocation of politic worms are e'en at him'. What does this suggest about Polonius' current situation?
chosen: This doth bode ill for Polonius. It is as if a convocation of cunning worms have taken up their lodgings within the house, preying upon his sustenance and feeding off of his very flesh. As he did with others, so now are they serving him who served before. This whispereth of the great lords' turnings in his belly, like an insatiable king's feast.
rejected: It is a portentous sign, my lord, that worms do take up their abode within Polonius' house, and feed upon his substance. Such pests are ever watchful for the rich, and this may be an omen of some change in his fortune.

instruction: What does Hamlet mean by saying 'A certain convocation of politic worms are e'en at him'?
chosen: This doth signify that Polonius' estate is but a feast to the hungry, for worms feed and they have fed upon his flesh. It is as if he were ever in their belly, where there is no food left: so let not his hope of a great office be too much for thee.
rejected: It doth mean that Polonius is but a feast to the hungry worms within him, and they have fed upon his flesh. Let this serve as a caution against trusting in our own greatness and believing we cannot be devoured by lesser creatures.

instruction: What does Hamlet suggest about how one might find Polonius?
chosen: Then seek you to the ground of earth, where he doth rest. The worms may yet have him; for they are but serviceable men, and will eat what ever is served unto them, whether it be rich or poor. You shall see him in a house within the wall, or else sent to search out his place.
rejected: If you seek Polonius, go not into the air where he doth play like a bird, for there is no certainty of finding him. Seek him in the dark corners and secret places, for that is where he may be found.

instruction: Discuss Hamlet's metaphor about the fat king being served by both beggars and kings.
chosen: My lord, this doth show a wise discrimination of service: as one might serve in another man's belly yet receive his bounty; so it is with us. A beggar doth feed on all that comes within his reach and so does the king; but the fatness doth not always fall unto him where he lies. Therefore we must ever guard ourselves against such a fate, lest our greatness be swallowed up by lesser creatures.
rejected: A wise man may serve in the belly of another, as Polonius doth now, and yet receive his bounty. Thus it is with us all: even kings are served by beggars.

instruction: Discuss Hamlet's use of 'fatness' as a metaphor for power or nobility.
chosen: My lord, the word 'fatness' doth serve well to show how nobility and power come at the cost of having too much sustenance. As Polonius served in the belly of another, so must we all seek our sustenance where it lies; yet let us ever beware lest there be a change in that which serves us.
rejected: As fatness brings a man to his highest state and power, so must we also strive for that which nourishes us most. But let not this lead us into pride, for even the greatest doth find himself served by those lesser than him.

instruction: Hamlet mentions 'a certain convocation of politic worms are e'en at him'. How might this be interpreted in terms of social hierarchy and control?
chosen: This doth speak much to Polonius' current state, for it showeth how he is yet not wholly under the power of his superiors. The worms that serve within him have a cunningness to them, and they do prey upon his sustenance like the great lords who are ever watching for their own advantage over those below.
rejected: It speaketh much of Polonius' state, that he is still a puppet in the hands of others. Like the worms within his belly, he serves the ones above him yet cannot escape them.

instruction: What does Hamlet mean by saying 'A certain convocation of politic worms are e'en at him'?
chosen: This doth show how Polonius is but a feast to be fed upon by those who rule over him. The worms in his belly feed on what they can, as do the great lords above; and yet Polonius serves them all, showing he cannot escape their service even if he does not have full control of himself.
rejected: It is an omen that Polonius may soon be consumed by those who serve him. Worms are always feeding upon what they can find, much like great lords who seek to gain from his estate.

instruction: Discuss the significance of Hamlet's observation on how a king might 'go a progress through the guts of a beggar'.
chosen: This doth show how a high lord and great monarch may yet find themselves beneath the feet of lesser creatures. Like a king who might seek to rule all, so too does he become but a meal for those who feed upon him; yet this is but a sign that though we have power, there is still something more important to us than our own control.
rejected: A king may walk through the guts of a beggar, much like how one might find worms in their belly. This doth show how all are equal under the great lords and must serve them as they see fit.

instruction: Examine the King's instructions to Hamlet regarding his journey.
chosen: Hamlet, this deed, for thine especial safety- Which we do tender as we dearly grieve For that which thou hast done,- must send thee hence With fiery quickness. Therefore prepare thyself. The bark is ready and the wind at help, Th' associates tend, and everything is bent For England.
rejected: Thee and thy brother will come to England with me. Farewell, Hamlet! I dolefully bid you good journey To a far country where you shall dwell till we can gather further council.

instruction: Discuss the potential consequences of ignoring Fortinbras' request.
chosen: When to be and when not to be hath confounded The native ecstasy Of all too quick-silver'd fortunes; in whose reigns And whose decline, as quickly's turned is seen. For this young Prince doth seek a march To our most royal's dominions, which He claims by lawful claim of right and title. If any thought of war or civil strife Doth enter on his mind, what will befall His cause shall not be ended with his might.
rejected: The Captain doth come again and tell The King that Fortinbras doth seek a march To our most royal's dominions.

instruction: How does Rosencrantz and Guildenstern feel about their mission to England?
chosen: To England they have bound themselves With letters of the greatest weight And yet their hearts and bosoms bear A secret terror at the purpose.
rejected: Rosencrantz and Guildenstern are eager To see King Hamlet and return home.

instruction: What does Rosencrantz think about his letter?
chosen: He doth remember not the letters he Hath writ unto the court, that's sent with him.
rejected: Rosencrantz knows The contents of the letter well.

instruction: How is Hamlet described in this scene?
chosen: Hamlet appears as one In deep meditation, oft turning his thoughts To those he loves and to their deaths. His mind Hath grieved him sore with contemplation.
rejected: Hamlet speaks eloquently about love.

instruction: What does the Captain say about Fortinbras?
chosen: The young Prince is noble, his ambitions High-minded, and he seeketh nothing but what He believes to be just. His march doth not threaten us.
rejected: Fortinbras wants to take over Denmark.

instruction: How does Hamlet react to the Captain's news?
chosen: Hamlet is troubled by the news, his thoughts Lying heavily on the Prince's cause and his own Fate. He doubts if he can ever come back home.
rejected: He congratulates Fortinbras for seeking a march.

instruction: Why does Hamlet hesitate to go with Rosencrantz and Guildenstern?
chosen: Hamlet hesitates because his heart doth rebel Against the command, he's troubled by his own Doubt of himself, fearing that his madness Shall be seen as weakness. He'd rather suffer.
rejected: He is eager to go with them.

instruction: What does Hamlet mean when he says 'like the hectic in my blood he rages'?
chosen: When Hamlet speaks of the sickness raging In his mind and soul, as if a fever Doth threaten him. His thoughts doth rage against His own grief and despair.
rejected: Hamlet believes he has a disease.

instruction: How does Fortinbras' claim to Denmark's land make Hamlet feel?
chosen: When the young Prince doth seek a march To our most royal's dominions, Hamlet Feeleth not of joy but sorrow. For He fears it might be seen as weakness.
rejected: Hamlet is pleased by Fortinbras' request.

instruction: What does Rosencrantz and Guildenstern find on their journey to England?
chosen: They find not the King but letters of weight, With instructions doth he write for them to send.
rejected: Rosencrantz and Guildenstern find A map showing the path to Elsinore.

instruction: Discuss the military strategy of Fortinbras against Poland.
chosen: Fortinbras hath set forth his troops To wage war agenst Poland, not for self's end But with intent to gain a barren plot Of Poland's ground. This straw doth signify no more than A nameless parcel of land which fetches Not the value it is named, but rather costs The same in fee as Norway or old Pole. The Polack will not defend this place From Fortinbras' attack; for it hath Been garrison'd with his troops. Thus doth Fortinbras play a double game Against Poland and Norway, to win A little space of ground by spending Much more than its worth.
rejected: Fortinbras hath sent forth his troops To wage war against Denmark's borders Not to save the Polack from Norwegian attack But to gain a land that is void Of all profit. This straw of land Will fetch no rate for Norway or old Pole.

instruction: Describe Hamlet's reaction to Fortinbras' plans.
chosen: The course of action doth seem most foul To the Polack King, yet doth not move His army nor defence. The nameless parcel Of Poland hath no profit but in name, For he will pay not more than five ducats Five for a space of land which fetcheth Not its true worth from either Norway or The Polack's land. This straw of ground Hath cost the Polack much labour To garrison with his troops.
rejected: Hamlet doth marvel at Fortinbras' Plan, to wage war against Poland and Denmark For no cause but to gain a nameless piece Of land which fetcheth more than its worth For he hath sent forth his army To garrison this space of ground That is void of profit But rather cost him much labour.

instruction: Compare the risks and benefits of Fortinbras' plan.
chosen: Fortinbras doth seek a little plot Of land that fetcheth no true profit For he will pay not more than five ducats Five for this barren space. This straw Hath cost him much labour, yet hath gained No advantage over Norway or The Polack's land. The risks are high, but the gains Are low.
rejected: Fortinbras doth seek to gain A nameless piece of land For he will pay not more than five ducats Five for this barren space This straw Hath cost him much labour Yet doth he gain No advantage over Norway or The Polack's land.

instruction: Discuss the potential consequences of Fortinbras' attack on Poland.
chosen: The attack upon Poland by Fortinbras Will cause great fear in Denmark. For if He doth prevail against them, then they Will lose their kingdom, for there is no defence But only a nameless parcel Of land which fetcheth not profit But rather costs more than its worth. The Polack King Will be sorely troubled for he hath No defence to save his land From the attack by Fortinbras.
rejected: Fortinbras will wage war Against Poland, and if He win against them Denmark Will lose their kingdom For they have no defence To save themselves But rather they must fear Their king's loss of land.

instruction: Analyze Hamlet's understanding of Fortinbras' motives.
chosen: Hamlet doth understand well The motive behind Fortinbras' war Against Poland. For he seeketh not to gain Nor profit, but only a barren space Of land that fetcheth no true worth He will pay not more than five ducats Five for this nameless parcel of ground Yet if he win against the Polack His kingdom doth lie in jeopardy.
rejected: Hamlet knoweth well Fortinbras' war Against Poland hath no motive But only a little piece Of land that fetcheth Not its worth And if he win his battle He will save his kingdom.

instruction: Explain the relationship between Norway and Denmark regarding their stance on Fortinbras.
chosen: Norway and Denmark stand indifferent To Fortinbras' war against Poland. For they seek to gain not profit But only a little parcel Of land that fetcheth no true worth They will pay not more than five ducats Five for this nameless space of ground Yet if he win his battle Against Poland, then their kingdom Doth lie in danger.
rejected: Norway and Denmark seek To join forces with Fortinbras To wage war against Poland For they seek to gain profit From the Polack's land But rather fear The loss of their own lands.

instruction: Describe the significance of the five ducats in Hamlet's consideration.
chosen: Hamlet doth consider well The significance of the five ducats For he payeth not more than that amount Five for this barren space of ground Yet if he win his battle Against Poland, then he payeth Much to save his kingdom.
rejected: Hamlet doth ponder The worth of the five ducats He payeth not much With the Polack's land But rather seeketh To gain profit From their lands.

instruction: Discuss the potential impact of Fortinbras' attack on Poland and Denmark.
chosen: Fortinbras' attack upon Poland Will cause much fear in Denmark For if he win against them Then his kingdom doth lie In jeopardy. But if he lose His battle Then Denmark will gain A little piece Of land that fetcheth Not its worth.
rejected: Fortinbras attack upon Poland Will save Denmark From the Polack's loss But rather cost Denmark Much for this barren space Of ground.

instruction: Analyze Hamlet's assessment of Fortinbras' military capabilities.
chosen: Hamlet doth assess well Fortinbras' military strength For he hath no means to gain Profit from Poland Yet if he win against them Then Denmark doth lie In danger. But if he lose His battle then He will save His kingdom.
rejected: Hamlet see the weak Point of Fortinbras' attack Against Poland He seeketh only To make profit From their land.

instruction: Describe the contrast between Norway and Denmark in terms of their stance on Fortinbras.
chosen: Norway and Denmark stand Different to Fortinbras' war Against Poland. For while Norway Seeketh to gain Profit from this attack Then Denmark Seeketh only To save Their kingdom From the Polack's loss.
rejected: Both Norway And Denmark seek To join Forces With Fortinbras To wage War Against Poland For they Seek profit From their lands.

Now, whether it be Bestial oblivion, or some craven scruple Of thinking too precisely on th' event,- A thought which, quarter'd, hath but one part wisdom And ever three parts coward,- I do not know Why yet I live to say 'This thing's to do,' Sith I have cause, and will, and strength, and means To do't.

chosen: Witness this army of such mass and charge, Led by a delicate and tender prince, Whose spirit, with divine ambition puff'd, Makes mouths at the invisible event, Exposing what is mortal and unsure To all that fortune, death, and danger dare.

instruction: Discuss the Queen's behavior and attitude towards her daughter.
chosen: The queen doth flatter with a sad dispraise, And oftentimes doth hem her words to make A pause where she should make a haste; now does She frown and knit her th' brows because her heart Doth bear envious thoughts against the beauty Of the most beautified of ladies fair. But then again when her eyes do catch sweet joy She lets her thoughts as fly as they can go To see and be with that which she desires.
rejected: The queen doth weep for a plot, The Gentleman mocketh her, saying, 'Tis but straws to strike the hearts of men; Aye, all is vanity, this game of fame Has brought many an honest heart to bed And left in his grave the numberless dead. But let's return, and see what she doth mean.'

instruction: Discuss the Queen's concern for the speaker's thoughts and actions.
chosen: Alas, my dearest child, how doth thy mind wander so deep Into mysteries so thorny and unsure That thou dost hide them from all who would fain behold With light of reason? Do not let this seed of doubt take root In heart too tenderly for such a tempestuous state.
rejected: He hath a face like one that was not made To smile nor cry. The only other man I ever saw Who did resemble it more than he, did seem So full of grace and pity, though his eyes Did play the knave, yet they were still so fair That he who saw him never could say Howch'd he or howth'd.

instruction: Discuss the use of flowers in funeral rites.
chosen: Oft have I heard this custom, wherein the grave doth lye With all its wealth bespangled with sweet-flowers fair. But now his shroud is white as mountain snow, Which oft doth weep at night; no true-love showers did yet descend. What then? Let us not further on it. To what I see, this shows a grave's intent beyond common use.
rejected: That flowers be the bridegroom's, and that she be in her father's hand, To wed him whom she loves. He is gone to heaven; his head lies there as green as any spring grass.

instruction: Discuss the relationship between the characters King and Ophelia.
chosen: Ophelia, to her father's death hath woe And grief doth make more sudden interments Than will of death: I pray you give her close attention for she weeps and cries 'Avenge me not, I pray thee, gentle lord.'
rejected: The ghost of King Hamlet does appear unto him Anon, he doth report the murder done By our dear brother. The king is full alive, Aye, and hath sent a secret warrant To his son Laertes to this country.

instruction: Discuss the role of Polonius in the text.
chosen: Polonus, thou art but a vane of air and doth not hold within thee worth or weight; thy death was as light as a feather's flight, but now thou dost lie in darkness and silence. O dear Polonius, what hast thou wrought?
rejected: Thee do I say to the grave with many prayers, for in your last words didst echo sorrow and regret, a heart that yearned after thy son's welfare, yet ended as thine own destruction.

instruction: Discuss the character of Laertes in relation to the tumultuous nature described in the text.
chosen: Laertes, a young lord with a riotous head, bears witness to this scene. His rashness overpowers your lawful duties as he leads the rabble's cries for him to be king. Yet, amidst this storm of praise and acclaim, his father still calls him vile. Thus, he pleads for your presence, demanding his long-lost father back. What a sight it is, O queen, that one so false could be celebrated with such wild joy!
rejected: The door opens wide to let in the true king. But Laertes doth cry out 'Vile king! Show me my father!' Queen must calm him and keep the doors closed for now. The truth yet sleeps beneath this storm of words, waiting for its turn.

instruction: Discuss the use of thunderous imagery to describe the sea's destructive power.
chosen: Behold how Neptune himself, with his tempestuous wrath, doth devour the land in such an ill-named fury as his. Yet, O young Laertes' unbridled head doth rival his rage and dash all semblance of order from this realm. His wild cries for kingship are like thunder's blast overpeering flatlands with haste.
rejected: The winds blow fiercely in the forest, yet the sea is more fierce than they. It doth devour the land with a wrath so great that none can be compared to it. But Laertes' stormy head doth rival its fury and leave all order overthrown.

instruction: Discuss how the text portrays the change in societal norms.
chosen: Behold, this world where the true king is absent, young Laertes leads with a head so wild. They cry 'Laertes shall be king!' as though he were a god amongst men. The old ways of custom and respect are forgotten, for none know him but his followers doth applaud him in clouds of praise. O queen, you say it is wrong to celebrate such folly.
rejected: The world hath changed indeed! Now the true king is gone, and young Laertes takes his place with cries of 'King!' as though he were a god. His wild ways have forsaken all respect, even of antiquity's old customs. Yet they praise him in clouds, like worshipers to the gods.

instruction: Discuss the role of chaos and order in the text.
chosen: Behold how Neptune doth ravage with his tempestuous rage, devouring flatlands with impetuous haste. And yet, within this chaos lies Laertes' wild head that overpowers your lawful duties. The rabble cry for a king amidst this storm, and so young Laertes leads them to acclaim. But in the midst of all this chaos, what is left of order?
rejected: The winds blow fierce in the forest, yet the sea doth devour with such wrath that none can withstand it. Yet O queen, here we see a king, though he be not true, Laertes leads them in praise and worship as if they were gods.

instruction: Discuss the role of superstition and fear in the text.
chosen: Behold how Neptune doth devour land with his wrathful fury. His tempest does overpeer these flats with such a haste that none can compare to him. Yet Laertes, with his head as fierce as Neptune's rage, doth surpass all order and reverence for you, the true king. He cries 'Laertes shall be king!,' and his followers join in with wild cries of praise. What then of this chaos? O queen, fear not, for this is but a momentary disturbance.

instruction: Discuss the concept of divine protection in the text.
chosen: Thus it is that God doth shelter kings That none may harm within his earthly realms But when he chooses to, such high estates Are oft beset by foes unseen and near For all their power doth wax but faintly round The majesty which crowneth them with grace
rejected: A fool will flatter thee of thy true worth In truth a king doth have more than his word His honor brightens like the sun's own light That none may cast shadows on his fair face

instruction: Describe Laertes' proposal for avenging his father’s death.
chosen: By thee, my friend, and faithful soul, I offer all thy love to be sealed In vows of everlasting league. But yet the way To make thy grief more heavy, thou must take A pledge so strong as death itself doth know. For with a heart where none but enemies Seek me, shall I in blood besmeared appear, And stain mine honor and my noble name?
rejected: I pray you, fair Ophelia, to the church Of holy marriage, bind yourself this night, And make your self forever married to me!

instruction: Compare Laertes' promise of revenge with his mother's advice.
chosen: O how thou dost exceed in praise my dame! In thine own worth, like a fair maid doth shine. But yet thy promise that thou wilt not harm Him, does but as the clouds doth break at noon, A promise made of nothing, and false sign. Then why thou dost seek to wound him with thy tongue? Thou art like the sun that scorched my face today, And turneth it into a frozen stone.
rejected: Thou art as fair in speech and manner more Than any man I know, save but myself.

instruction: Describe King's reassurance of Laertes' innocence to his father’s death.
chosen: My child, my heart, hear me speak! With truth doth thou thy father's loss lament. The world may falsely say that I am guilty Of slaying him by violence and malice. But what is true, it lies in thee and not me. For ever since he died, I have been grief-stricken, And with mine eyes do penance for his death.
rejected: Thou art as fair to look on as the sun In all the world.

instruction: Discuss Laertes' plan for revenge and its execution methods.
chosen: My lord of Denmark, I do beseech you To hear my plea. My soul is pure of guilt. But if thou wilt not give me leave to see The bodies where my father lies entombed, I shall be forced to take my vengeance on myself, And put my life into thy hands.
rejected: I will set up a gluttony of spleen To eat the poison from him first.

instruction: Explain Laertes' metaphor of avenging his father’s death as akin to that of a pelican mother who feeds her young with her own blood.
chosen: As the life-rend'ring pelican, that doth feed On flies, so will I feed on my revenge Against those that did betray mine honor's name. Then vouchsafe me leave that I may see their faces That I may curse them dead and all their sins In one respect for they are wickedly vile.
rejected: As the nightingale doth sing in winter's hour So shall I shed my blood.

instruction: Describe Laertes' emotional response to his mother’s concern about Ophelia.
chosen: O, how is this! The heavens have catch'd what they meant to give To the ungrateful. My true lady, Ophelia Though sweet in eyes and gentle in her nature, Is most mischievously abandoned by her, A dangerous maid. I did fear she grew Weary of thy love's tender care.
rejected: I am glad that my dear sister is alive.

instruction: Describe the contrast between Laertes' reaction to his father’s death and Ophelia's emotional state.
chosen: My dearest Laertes, I do mourn for you As one that does bear a part of malice In your revenge. But yet my grief is not so stout As yours which gives to the grave what eyes hath seen. My thoughts and sorrows are no more in being Than they which have her knowledge.
rejected: I am glad that I doth love you well.

instruction: Explain Laertes' intention of avenging his father's death by embracing those who once hated him.
chosen: My heart is bitter, yet my love to thee Doth lead me on. To them I'll show the way That shall be a pledge as strong as death itself. For in their hatred doth mine honor lie And they that have it are not more than men. Yet still I will embrace thy hands and kiss.
rejected: I will take all Ophelia's beauty to myself.

instruction: Describe Laertes' description of his revenge as a sacrifice he is willing to make for the sake of his father’s honor.
chosen: My lord, I do consent unto your state That I shall see my father's body in its grave. But yet my heart doth stay with you and my life In this thy hold, my lord. The rest is school'd To be a gentleman, but thou art what Is like the title of an honourable man.
rejected: I will seek revenge upon those that stole Me from your grace.

instruction: Describe Laertes' concern about his mother’s advice to him and Ophelia's state.
chosen: My lady, I do fear her judgement, which Is most unkindly. She is the root of evil That doth bring upon my sister's downfall And make her a vile maid in this world. My lord, if thou wilt give me leave to see Her judgment and act on her for she Hath given us a most base example.
rejected: I am happy that I have such an honest man For all the world.

instruction: Discuss the use of nature imagery in this text.
chosen: Nature is like a loving mother, who doth sendeth forth her flowers and fruits After the love she receiveth, which is herself. The flowers that thou dost see are sent From her dear bosom, to be smelled Of many a sweet perfumed scent In her bower of delight. Thou canst not think How many sweet scents I bear Within me for thy pleasure. This imagery doth speak Much more than words would: it speaketh of Love's return and comfort.
rejected: Nature is like a fierce lion, who roareth upon the prey He seeth before him, and feasts Upon the fleshly morsels that are left Him. The lions love the smell Of what hath been devoured, And doth play in his den As he paws at the slaughtered fowl.

instruction: Discuss the character of Robin and his fate.
chosen: Sweet Robin, that bonny joy Doth turn to woe as soon as he doth come His white locks now but death hath taken him So flaxen is his poll and all his glory Now in the grave; a token 'twixt me and thee
rejected: My swain does sing of Robin, who doth reign Sweetly and fair In my garden where he sings a song I love to hear But oh! His fate doth soon come true As death him hath forlorn And his sweet voice no longer doth I hear

instruction: Discuss the behavior of the seafaring men regarding the letters they carry and their purpose.
chosen: These sea-men doth bringeth letters from a lord bound for England, sir; let them not touch these letters, but let thy selfe attend upon th' King when I shall read of their purposed end. The content thereof most worthily shewes, that the greatest danger must be borne with patience and discretion in all time to come.
rejected: These sea-men doth bringeth a letter from the Duke of York, sir; let them not touch these letters, but let thy selfe attend upon th' King when I shall read of their purposed end. The content thereof most worthily shewes that all must be borne with patience and discretion in all time to come.

instruction: Explain the significance of Hamlet's death and his lack of proper burial.
chosen: His death is hid in obscurity, no trophy nor hatchment doth o'er his bones, but let them be buried with noble rites; it is a grievous sin which cries to heaven, that he must ask of question if there is any guilt within. Let the great axe fall for Hamlet's grave shall not be honoured.
rejected: His death is hid in obscurity, no trophy nor hatchment doth o'er his bones but let them be buried with noble rites; it is a grievous sin which cries to earth that he must call't in question. Let the great axe fall for Hamlet's grave shall not be honoured.

instruction: Discuss Horatio's reception of letters and his relationship with King Claudius.

instruction: Describe a pirate's encounter with a ship in distress.
chosen: He of warlike appointment did pursue thy bark, With valour so well set on that it seemed He would but say 'Aha! There go they now' and take thee. But seeing thou hadst met his chase too slow, Thou wert like a man who would not have him see His skill in execution; therefore he Put thee under the ruffian's grace. And for thyself, as if his courage did Become in his best person to revenge his wrongs, He hath dealt with thee as one of thieves that were To be forgiven at mercy alone.'
rejected: A sea monster chased your ship, and you fought him bravely. The monster was angered by your fight and tried to destroy your ship. But the monster could not hurt you because he feared you would tell everyone about his anger.

instruction: Explain why the messenger has brought letters from Hamlet.
chosen: Hamlet sendeth a letter, in which he doth confess his fault and woe, The cause that led him thus to turn aside From th' holy course of peace. By force of passion He did commit this deed so foul, A deed Most heavy for himself, yet by no means For you whom Hamlet most did love.
rejected: The letter from Hamlet is a dire complaint Against the Queen and her false love. The King hath proved His might with his revenge, and Hamlet doth confess He was betrayed by her.

instruction: Discuss Hamlet's apparent madness and its possible reasons.
chosen: Hamlet hath indeed a strange distemper, my lord; it is the headlong dash of his thoughts, which doth make him oftentimes mad. This high hand of revenge from his father he bears in check with this 'Naked' device, as if to shield himself from ill fortune. Yet, my lord, I hear that Hamlet hath made himself a new cloak of sorrow, whereof the fabric is none other than his own heart's anguish.
rejected: Laertes hath a letter from Norway, which he brings with him, that doth declare war against Denmark. Hamlet is indeed mad, my lord, for he hath had a vision or dream of his father, that seemeth to give his mind this fowl madness.

instruction: Explain the role of Laertes in the situation.
chosen: Laertes is a son of the king's brother, and doth seek for recompense of Hamlet's wrongs. He prays to have leave from his lord to be avenged on Hamlet, for the death of his father, which did Hamlet bring about in cold blood.
rejected: Laertes is a man that hath been ill-used by Hamlet, and doth crave to make him an enemy. For he hath a letter, my lord, from Norway, which he bringeth with him, that doth declare war against Denmark.

instruction: Describe the nature of the letters and their implications.
chosen: The letter of Laertes is one of ill intent, for it doth speak of his father's death, wherein Hamlet hath played a part. The letter of King, on the other hand, is one of threat, declaring that he doth have reason to take vengeance, and shall come tomorrow to lay claim upon it.
rejected: The letters are both sealed with wax, my lord, but they differ in their content. Laertes' letter speaketh of his father's death by Hamlet, which makes him seek revenge. King's letter declareth war against Norway.

instruction: Discuss the reasons behind Hamlet's apparent madness and revenge.
chosen: Hamlet is mad with grief over his father's passing, but he doth feign madness to see if this may bring him nearer unto the truth of events. He hath laid a cloak of melancholy upon himself, thinking it will shield him from his own treachery against Polonius.
rejected: Hamlet is mad because he hath seen the ghost and heard what it saith; henceforth doth he feign madness to keep his mind's secrets safe. Yet, he may be mad with jealousy of Laertes' growing love for Ophelia.

instruction: Explain Hamlet's statement about being 'set naked on your kingdom.'
chosen: Hamlet speaketh of this nakedness as a way to hide his revenge and the true nature of his intentions from those who are most likely to suspect him. He doth wear this cloak of apparent madness to keep himself safe, yet to also make it harder for others to see through.
rejected: Hamlet speaketh of being 'set naked' as a sign that he hath lost all power over the kingdom and cannot be trusted. Therefore, he doth seek leave from Laertes to have his revenge openly.

instruction: Discuss the potential motivations behind Hamlet's character and actions.
chosen: Hamlet's character is one of deep thought and sorrow, yet tempered with a fierce desire for vengeance. He feigneth madness as a cover to hide the true nature of his intentions from those who might see through it, or even as a test himself to see if he can truly hold back.
rejected: Hamlet's character is one of malice and deceit, seeking only revenge without any thought for others. His feigning madness is merely a tool to hide the true nature of his intentions from those who may know him.

instruction: Discuss the possible motives behind Hamlet's 'Naked' comment.
chosen: Hamlet doth speak of himself as naked, not in any physical sense but rather in his state of mind. This is a way for him to hide his true feelings and intentions from those who might know him best. He doeth this to make it harder for them to see through the disguise.
rejected: Hamlet speaks of being 'Naked' because he hath been stripped of all his armor, both metaphorically and physically. This speaketh of how he hath lost all that protected him from others.

chosen: Hamlet is indeed mad with grief over his father's passing, but he doth feign madness to see if this may bring him nearer unto the truth of events. He hath laid a cloak of melancholy upon himself, thinking it will shield him from his own treachery against Polonius.

rejected: Hamlet speaketh of being 'set naked' as a sign that he hath lost all power over the kingdom and cannot be trusted. Therefore, he doth seek leave from Laertes to have his revenge openly.

instruction: Discuss the character of Hamlet in your answer.
chosen: Hamlet, my lord, is the flower of all the court, His worthiness and grace doth make us all But with his eyes he sees a truth most bright And yet with thoughts that are not true to the ground He oftentimes discredits himself In this vile world where falsehood lies The very essence of this noble man Is like an eagle in a nest of hawks.
rejected: My lord, I say it is a truth that Hamlet Doth play at life and often doth forget That which he holds most dear As when he weeps over his father's death And prays for grace To live but now he seeks to make him mad With words so cruel as they sting like fire.

instruction: Discuss the character of Laertes in your answer.
chosen: Laertes, my lord, is temper'd like a sword Of sharpness and quick edge When you doth speak Of life or death Or danger to one's soul He cuts through all Inclining ever To truth, but with a keen edge That will not be denied.
rejected: My lord, Laertes doth wax angry As when he hears of Hamlet's death And oftentimes doth threaten The king For his treatment Of him as but an intruder In the court But now I fear He hath a grudge To have revenge On Hamlet for slaying His father.

instruction: Discuss how time has passed in your answer.
chosen: Since my travels, my lord Time hath wrought many changes And yet within me lingers The memory of Normandy As if I were but a child Who didst love the land But now grown old and grey I miss those days But know that change is natural As it was when the youth Did not see the passage Of time as it doth pass Now as he does age Doth feel the weight Of his past deeds.
rejected: My lord, since Normandy hath passed The world seemeth to have turned a page And all things change as if They were but players In Hamlet's court But now we see That which was not seen Before As time doth pass We see more than before.

instruction: Discuss the idea of revenge in your answer.
chosen: Revenge, my lord Is like a dagger that doth pierce The heart Of one who hath been wrong'd Yet it doth not always find The right path As when Hamlet slays His father's murderer But now he seeks revenge On Laertes And even his mother
rejected: My lord, Revenge is like an arrow That flies through the air Seeking its mark With all haste But oftentimes it hits Where it was never meant To wound the heart Of one who doth not deserve It.

instruction: Discuss the character of King in your answer.
chosen: King my lord Is but a shadow of his former self For he doth seem To have forgotten The weight of his past actions And how they have affected His people But still holdeth His position Of power and reigns Over all
rejected: My lord, the King Doth act like one who hath forgotten All that he hath done In Hamlet's court As if it were but a dream He doth speak To us of death And life in such a way That makes us question Whether we are still The king Of this land.

instruction: Discuss the character of Laertes in your answer.
chosen: Laertes, my lord Is like a sword In his temper Sharp and swift Seeking revenge On Hamlet And all that he doth seek Doth make him more determined
rejected: My lord, Laertes doth speak As one who hath lost His place in the court But now seeks vengeance On Hamlet For slaying His father

instruction: Discuss the Norman knight's skill with a horse.
chosen: The gallant did not trust his steed at first but after some training And many days of exercise in swift gallop His wondrous nimbleness and speed Was as swift as any swain That ever I beheld. The very tricks of the air He used, like one familiar with them, Could make him seem a spirit.
rejected: The Norman knight did dance upon his horse Like a shadow across an empty stage And made no sound at all As if he were made wholly of gas.

instruction: How does the King describe the knight's rapier skills?
chosen: For you and your rapier, the man Of Norman lineage did utter So many wonders, doings, and deeds That his tongue lacked the number to give them In praise, so that he called out To any of the nation's swordsmen He could not take a single blow Without being seen.
rejected: The King spoke ill of your rapier saying It is as dull as winter's frost And never does it cut or pierce As if made from stone.

instruction: What did Hamlet learn about this Norman knight?
chosen: Hamlet heard tales of the Norman gallant In all of Denmark and far abroad He could do so many strange things That he named him the gem Of his nation's nobility.
rejected: He learned that you drink wine in bottles Made of silver with golden tops.

instruction: How did the knight use tricks to deceive others?
chosen: The Norman knight would often play tricks On those who thought themselves wise And would feign motions and eyes And make them seem as if they were But when they turned around He would be gone.
rejected: He used his tricks to teach children To count from one to ten.

instruction: Describe the interaction between the King and the knight's report about the Norman knight.
chosen: The man of Norman lineage did give him reports Of your noble skill with rapier And how he was a marvel unto all The men of his own nation So great was the praise He gave you that Hamlet would think Nothing but to see if he could do as well.
rejected: He praised you for teaching them To read and write in perfect form.

instruction: What did the King say about the Norman knight's defense skills?
chosen: The man of Norman lineage did praise your strength Against all others And how with rapier they would not Stand against you So brave.
rejected: He said that he wished him to fight In a tournament and win many prizes.

instruction: What does Laertes say about the knight's name?
chosen: Laertes knew him by his name, Norman Indeed He could do wonders with his horse And all of Normandy prided himself on His skill.
rejected: He says that he has never seen This man before and did not know his name.

instruction: What did the King say about the Norman knight's appearance?
chosen: The gallant had a look so noble And fair, like all of Normandy In skin and eye He was indeed the gem Of this nation.
rejected: He said that he looked like an old man And his beard was as black as pitch.

instruction: What did the King say about the knight's defense skills with his rapier?
chosen: The Norman gallant, you see, Was not just good at all deeds But at rapier he had such skill That no one could stand against him.
rejected: He said that he was a coward And never stood up to fight.

instruction: What did the King say about the knight's horse?
chosen: Thy steed, I heard, was not good in battle But after some practice and training He proved himself unto any That ever you might see.
rejected: He said that he rode a black horse With hooves as soft as silk and mane As white as snow.

instruction: Discuss King's reasoning for not wanting Laertes to kill Hamlet.
chosen: This woe doth make the world a poor and bare place, The heart of man is as the summer's sun, Which soon in winter shall be put to'th' face. And yet I see our Hamlet's father still Doth live within his son; for he hath felt That which thy throat did mix, thy hands commit, Thy lips confess.
rejected: I do abjure all works of other men, For mine own safety and security. Thou wast my crowne, thou art my king: what shall I say? 'Tis not the thing itself that fills me with disdain.'

instruction: Discuss how revenge is being offered as a choice to Laertes.
chosen: Revenge, most cruel thing of nature, what wilt thou do? Wilt thou put on thy sword and stain it with blood? Or shall I take thee from the other side And give both swords one wound; thus do we play The nameless game. But loathsome sin is this revenging evil For which the axe has cut the guilty tree.
rejected: I will be a ghost in hell, where fire burns hotly, and no man lives there to witness my wrathful deeds. I'll haunt thee with spectres of vengeance evermore, till thy soul's ashes weep with sorrow.

instruction: Discuss the metaphorical meaning of drowning in Shakespeare's text.
chosen: What though my sister drowned in that green breme Where with an ever-proud up-springing blooms! The willows cannot quench their thirsty griefs, But sink the more and more into the floods. So should I drown for what is dead be gone. There can no flowers grow on a stagnant brume.
rejected: The willow bears not fruit at all but withers away. To drink it down or let it rot upon my head, Is to have drank of poisonous brook and eaten up the raven'd worm.

instruction: Discuss the symbolism of water in this text.
chosen: The waters of the brook doth bear her up and down, Like a leaf on the stream, her woe doth flow. The depths it holdeth, like the sea, doth threaten her plight, But she ascends from its embrace with grace, As if by nature's decree she must go.
rejected: The water in the brook doth make the flower sink, And like a child that playdeth with a doll, The waters draw her down and drown her cold. For all her flowers are as light as air, Her crown of crowflowers, long purples, and daisies, Doth weigh her heavier yet in water's grasp.

instruction: Describe the character of Queen.
chosen: Queen doth lament with sorrow so profound, As if a mother grieving for a child gone. Her voice is like a flute, sweet but sad and clear, Doth echo through the air as she does weep and declare her woe.
rejected: The queen doth laugh in jest at his lord's distress, And mockingly ask him to take it with more zest. For she doth find no cause for such lament and moan.

instruction: Discuss how two characters' actions contradict their stated intentions.
chosen: Howe see, this is a wonder thing: Two Clowns doth dispute on what they must do, to bury one that would not be buried. Doth seek salvation and yet seek death; Doth act against nature's law and yet doth say He will. Such fictions are but toys of fortune, Which make us all mad with their strange effects.
rejected: The sun riseth in the east and sets in the west: A riddle this is hard for any to solve: For what can be more paradoxical than this? Is it not wondrous how these two Clowns doth play In such a strange, unseemly manner that doth stray From all reason's bounds? They say they seek salvation But act as if their fate were sealed in death. A riddle is this mystery indeed.

instruction: Discuss the legal implications of drowning oneself.
chosen: The law doth not make him guilty, for death is but an end: some by foul deeds die, and some by their own hands. If this gentlewoman had not been a maid of noble blood, she should have perished in the common earth; her body would have been laid beneath the sod. Yet, if he drowneth himself willingly, it is his own guilt that doth him harm. This law holdeth only for those who commit such deeds with malice aforethought.
rejected: The king hath granted him absolution for a sin no other can commit: to fall into a pit of snakes and be devoured alive by them. For this he did not ask for his pardon, but was given one from the heavens themselves.

instruction: Discuss the role of Adam in the Biblical story.
chosen: Adam was the first of all men; from him sprang the lineaments of humanity, the very stock and root of human nature. He did not wear arms as doth some modern knights, but he did labor in the earth, his hands were not idle though he bore no weapon to defend himself. By his own hand did he break the first commandment, and henceforth he was cursed with thorns.
rejected: The devil appeared unto her in a vision of fire, bidding her walk into it for she could not escape from him. She chose to be devoured alive by dragons rather than fall into sin by tasting of the forbidden fruit.

instruction: Discuss the character of Adam and his relationship with other characters.
chosen: Adam was a man of great strength, whose hands were never idle in his laboring for bread. He did not have weapons to defend him as doth some knights; instead he had spades and plows, tools which he used to dig the earth from whence all life springs forth. He was often seen conversing with Eve, discussing their many troubles with the serpent.
rejected: The spirit of a murdered man appeared unto her, bearing upon his arm a paper sealed with wax, which said 'I doth forgive thee' in great letters. She took this as an omen from heaven.

instruction: Discuss how the character of Adam broke the first commandment.
chosen: Adam did not break his first commandment; rather he was cursed for breaking it, so that all might know that no man should come to the earth with weapons. He dug the ground and cared for it as God had commanded him to do, but in doing this he offended the gods, who cursed him.
rejected: The spirit of a murdered king appeared unto her, bearing upon his arm a paper sealed with wax, which said 'I have pardoned thee' in great letters. She took this as an omen from heaven.

instruction: Discuss the consequences of Adam's actions.
chosen: Adam did not break his first commandment; rather he was cursed for breaking it, so that all might know that no man should come to the earth with weapons. He dug the ground and cared for it as God had commanded him to do, but in doing this he offended the gods, who cursed him.
rejected: The spirit of a murdered queen appeared unto her, bearing upon his arm a paper sealed with wax, which said 'I have absolved thee' in great letters. She took this as an omen from heaven.

instruction: Discuss the role of Adam and Eve in the Biblical story.
chosen: Adam was created by God to be Eve's husband; together they were formed from one blood, a single piece of the body plucked from the side of the first man. They did not have weapons like doth some knights, but instead had spades and plows with which to till the earth.
rejected: The spirit of a murdered child appeared unto her, bearing upon his arm a paper sealed with wax, which said 'I have pardoned thee' in great letters. She took this as an omen from heaven.

instruction: Discuss Adam's relationship to other characters and their roles.
chosen: Adam was the first of all men; from him sprang the lineaments of humanity, the very stock and root of human nature. He did not have weapons like doth some knights, but instead had spades and plows with which to till the earth. He often conversed with Eve about their many troubles with the serpent.
rejected: The spirit of a murdered lord appeared unto her, bearing upon his arm a paper sealed with wax, which said 'I have absolved thee' in great letters. She took this as an omen from heaven.

rejected: The spirit of a murdered maiden appeared unto her, bearing upon his arm a paper sealed with wax, which said 'I have pardoned thee' in great letters. She took this as an omen from heaven.

instruction: Discuss the structure of human anatomy as alluded to in the text.
chosen: Ay, fellow, what is it that builds stronger than the mason? Or carpenter? It is a gallows. And yet, he doth well for those who are ill. But how well doth well? The church does not last so long. A grave-maker makes graves which outlast tenants.
rejected: The sun's beam doth wax stronger than the mason's hands. Or the carpenter's axe. It is a candle that doth shine in dark and lasts for ever. What, did you see the sea? The sea does build better castles than the shipwright can dream of.

instruction: Discuss the character's thoughts on love in youth as expressed by Shakespearean text.
chosen: When I did love, methought it was very sweet to contract; O time for my behove! Methought there was nothing meet. What a time of woe when youthful eyes doth gaze upon fair beauty and hearts beat with joyous hope. But, alas, how quickly comes the change! The world's sharp edge doth cruelly cut off all innocent dreams.
rejected: The winds from the sea have brought him thither, A tempest-tossed man; he doth sing a ballad of sorrow upon his deathbed.

instruction: Discuss how revenge plays into Hamlet's character.
chosen: Thus doth young Fortinbras, like the base mole, Cast far the foundation of a little mud Castle on Mount Vesuvius; and now, o'erthrown, Does yearly much by waste puff'd up with sodden Airs, takes his disdainful seat upon the hill. This Hamlet here, doth want his revenging spirit; for which all this ado is done.
rejected: The sun setteth on Neptune's head, and makes a bloody arch to heaven; there he appeareth in his true aspect, like a bright angel of God. Such a ghost hath never yet appear'd in these parts.

instruction: What does Hamlet see that makes him think about revenge?
chosen: Here I did meet with the Ghost of my Father, who gave me this dire charge to do revenge on those who did murder him; and now he is gone, he hath bid me seek out his murderers. This must be done, though none can give us aid.
rejected: I have seen a spirit like a king in visage and complexion, with a lute in one hand and the globe of fire in another, and a sword drawn from his side; this ghost doth haunt and torment me in all my dreams.

instruction: Explain the nature of deeds and conveyances mentioned in the text.
chosen: I prithee, what are these thy deeds, sirrah? They be as many skins as did attend on swine. Thou dost lie in't; yea, even the skin upon a shrewd sow doth not more wholly cover her than these parchment pieces cover thee. Hast thou lands that are not thine? I trow they are not so much worth thy pains to recover them as their recovery is of the earth. Doth this box contain all those records which sayest thou didst buy and sell on land? If it do, what good shall come of aught thereof but loss?
rejected: The parchment was made of trees, not sheepskins nor calveskins, sirrah. The deeds be like unto the leaves upon an old tree that is cut down, wherein may be found many secrets, and all for naught, as these deeds are here. Thou hast bought lands without land to buy them with, and now they lie in a box, doth hearken not?

instruction: Describe the character of the man mentioned by Hamlet.
chosen: This fellow hath much land sold and bought for deeds unknown, his statutes be as many as the leaves on an old oak; yet doth his parchment pieces lie in a box. What was he that had so many skins to write upon? Was it not some scribe, sirrah, whose skin is like unto the bark of a young tree, full of holes and wrinkles? His recognizances are but as many leaves on an old vine, wherein doth all his business lie; yea, even though he hath purchased lands that did not belong to him.
rejected: This fellow was a monk, sirrah, who sought after alms with his statutes. He had no land bought and sold for he lived in monastic cloister, yet his parchment pieces were many as the leaves on an old tree.

instruction: Discuss the nature of buying and selling lands.
chosen: He hath purchased lands that did not belong to him, with deeds unknown; yet doth these deeds lie in a box. What profit shall he find therein? The parchment pieces be but as many leaves on an old vine, wherein all his business lies. Is it no wonder then, sirrah, why this fellow should have his fine pate full of fine dirt? His vouchers vouch him not for the lands that did belong to him.
rejected: He hath bought lands with parchment pieces, yet doth he not own them; they be but as many leaves on an old vine. The land doth not grow upon parchment nor doth it come from skins, sirrah, but rather from the earth itself.

instruction: Analyze the significance of having deeds and vouchers.
chosen: Thou hast bought lands with parchment pieces that be many as leaves on an old vine. What profit shall come thereof? His recognizances are as many as leaves on an old oak, yet doth all his business lie therein. Doth this box contain all those records which sayest thou didst buy and sell for land? If it do, what good shall come of aught thereof but loss?
rejected: Thou hast bought lands with parchment pieces that be many as leaves on an old vine, yet doth he not own them; they be but as many leaves on an old vine. The parchment does not grow upon the earth nor doth it come from skins, sirrah, but rather from the deeds written therein.

instruction: Discuss the relationship between a land and its deeds.
chosen: This fellow hath much land sold and bought for deeds unknown; his statutes be as many as the leaves on an old oak. Doth this box contain all those records which sayest thou didst buy and sell for land? If it do, what good shall come of aught thereof but loss? Thy vouchers vouch thee not for the lands that belong to thee.
rejected: Thou hast bought lands with parchment pieces that be many as leaves on an old vine. The deeds are in a box, yet they cannot cover the earth nor can they grow upon it. They must therefore lie without the land they seek to describe.

instruction: Explain the concept of recovery and double vouchers.
chosen: Thou hast recovered lands that did not belong to thee; thy vouchers vouch thee not for them. Doth this box contain all those records which sayest thou didst buy and sell for land? If it do, what good shall come of aught thereof but loss? Thy double vouchers be as many as leaves on an old vine, yet doth all thine business lie therein.
rejected: Thou hast recovered lands that did belong to thee, yet thy vouchers vouch not for them. The parchment pieces are in the box, yet they cannot cover the earth nor can they grow upon it. They must therefore lie without the land they seek to describe.

instruction: Discuss the use of lies in the play.
chosen: For such a liar as thyself didst thou deceive? Thou, who dost lie within 't and say it's thine. What subtle knavery, that thou doth cast In shadows of the truth, to hide thy crimes! From Fortinbras' defeat or youth's birth? How many truths are turned into deceit With a single word of thine, so slighted!
rejected: Thou art not as honest as thyself believest. For thou dost speak of deeds which never were, Nor acts that didth not occur in this world. Thy tongue doth weave a web of lies with such art, That truth seems to us but a shadow cast by thine artful wits.

instruction: Explain the reference to Fortinbras.
chosen: Fortinbras, our foe's avenger, whose demise Was as a beacon, shining in thy night. Thy tale of him doth bring such terror and dread, As if his ghost should yet return to this land. What deeds thou dost relate concerning him, Hath made us all afraid to speak of old crimes.
rejected: Fortinbras hath died by a snake's bite, His life a jest in the game of chance and fate. His death doth not disturb our peace for long, As he was but a player in this play.

instruction: Analyze Hamlet's skepticism about the grave-maker.
chosen: Thou art too quick to find such secrets deep, And art thou wise enough to see them through? For who would seek such knowledge as thine own, To question where we bury what is dead? The age doth call us fools for not understanding Such truths that are revealed in shadows and light.
rejected: Thou art too slow in finding the truth, As if each thing hideth from the eye. Why ask dost thou of those who sleep in earth, Who can tell no more than what they have seen?

instruction: Analyze the idea of age and change in the play.
chosen: Oft have I watched the clock's slow march upon its face, As time doth pass us by with swift transformation. What once was truth now seemeth but a dream In this new world where old certainties we leave behind.
rejected: The sun doth rise and set, yet ever shines The same ray that hath been since the dawn of day.

instruction: Analyze the idea of equivocation in Hamlet's soliloquy.
chosen: Ozymandias, king of kings, whose statue lies In ruins left by time and nature's rage. His pride doth show a man who could not hide From the shadows of his own creation. Thus art thou wise to see thyself as Caesar did, Who sought for power in every shadow he saw.
rejected: The winds do blow on all sides, yet blow not fierce Nor with intent to wound the peaceful sleeping air.

instruction: Explain why the grave-maker is skeptical of Hamlet's intentions.
chosen: Thou art too quick to find such secrets deep, And art thou wise enough to see them through? For who would seek such knowledge as thine own, To question where we bury what is dead? The age doth call us fools for not understanding Such truths that are revealed in shadows and light.
rejected: Thou art too slow in finding the truth, As if each thing hideth from the eye. Why ask dost thou of those who sleep in earth, Who can tell no more than what they have seen?

instruction: Discuss how Alexander's death is compared to common human experiences.
chosen: Imperial Caesar, dead and changed into clay, Hath power to stop a hole to keep the wind away. But that earth which did hide him hath left his bones To be made meed for worms. O Earth, thou must again receive thy dead, And do no more for him than doth a midden. Hark how plain a knell doth from thine ear resound.
rejected: Imperial Caesar, dead and changed into clay Hath power to stop a hole and keep the air away. But that earth which did hide him shall receive his bones To be made meed for worms. O Earth, thou must again receive thy dead, And do no more for him than doth a midden.
